Plastics are a heat problem, not a strength problem: acrylic (Plexiglas) melts and re-welds behind the blade or chips and cracks if attacked fast; use a fine or plastic-specific blade, slow speed, zero orbit, gentle feed, and leave protective film on; if the kerf melts closed, slow down further — some workers run a bead of water or cut sandwiched between sacrificial hardboard. PVC pipe and trim cut easily at low speed. Non-ferrous metals — aluminum sheet, plate, and profiles, brass, copper — want 12 to 24 TPI metal blades depending on thickness, slow speed, zero orbit, and a drop of cutting oil or even candle wax on the blade; aluminum loads gullets, so clear chips often. Steel sheet up to a few millimeters is a legitimate jigsaw job with a 21 to 24 TPI bi-metal blade, lowest speed, zero orbit, oil, and patience — expect slow progress and a hot workpiece; thin sheet under about one millimeter should be sandwiched between plywood or hardboard scraps so the teeth always have three in contact and the sheet cannot chatter and tear. Ceramic wall tile (not dense porcelain) yields to a carbide-grit blade at low speed with water sponged on to cool and suppress dust; cuts are slow and edges need rubbing smooth. Fiber-cement siding demands a carbide blade, extraction, and a proper respirator because its dust contains crystalline silica. Two universal habits close the table: let the blade reach full speed before touching the work, and let the saw finish the stroke fully before withdrawing from an incomplete kerf, or the snagging blade will kick the workpiece and bend or break.

sections.heading: Setting Up: Saw, Blade, and a Kit That Covers Most Jobs
sections.body: Five minutes of setup prevents most jigsaw failures, and the routine is always the same. Unplug the saw or remove its battery before touching the blade — reciprocating tools have no forgiving direction. Fit the right blade for the material and confirm it clicks home fully in the clamp and seats in the groove of the guide roller behind it; a blade riding outside the roller will cut bevels you did not ask for. Sight down the blade from the front: it should stand square to the shoe, and if a previous job bent it even slightly, discard it — a bent blade cannot cut straight and costs less than the wood it ruins. Check the shoe: locked at exactly zero for square cuts (verify occasionally with a small square against the blade, because bevel locks drift), the anti-splinter insert fitted for fine face work, the plastic overshoe on for scratch-prone surfaces, off for maximum stability on rough ones. Set orbit and speed for the material, connect dust extraction if the saw has a port or switch on the blower so the line stays visible, and put on safety glasses — a jigsaw throws chips upward, directly toward the face, and hearing protection is sensible for any extended session. Then check the path under the cut: the blade projects below the work by the stroke length plus spare blade, and it will happily saw into the sawhorse, the cable, or the second layer of the sheet; drape the cord over a shoulder or use a cordless saw, and confirm nothing but air sits beneath the line. A modest kit covers nearly every household job, and it is worth assembling once rather than improvising each time. The essentials the text that follows assumes are listed here, and none is exotic: all are stocked by any hardware store or online tool retailer, and the total cost is small compared to a single cabinet-grade sheet of plywood.
ingredients: A jigsaw with variable speed, orbital settings, tool-less T-shank clamp, and a tilting shoe; cordless is convenient, corded is fine

Assorted T-shank blades: coarse 6 TPI wood, general 10 TPI wood, fine-finish ground 10-12 TPI, scroll blades for tight curves, 21-24 TPI bi-metal for metal, reverse-tooth for laminate, carbide-grit for tile or cement board
Two quick-grip clamps and two G-clamps or screw clamps for workholding
A pair of sawhorses or a portable workbench, plus rigid foam insulation board as a full-sheet cutting bed
Marking tools: sharp pencils, a fine marker for dark or rough stock, a utility knife for scoring veneers, masking tape
Layout tools: combination square, tape measure, a compass or improvised string-and-pencil trammel, a flexible batten or thin strip for fair curves
A drill with twist and spade bits (6-12 mm) for starter holes in interior cutouts
Safety kit: safety glasses, hearing protection, a dust mask or respirator rated for fine dust, and dust extraction or a shop vacuum where possible
Cutting lubricant for metal (cutting oil, or a wax candle rubbed on the blade), and abrasives, files, and a sanding block for edge cleanup

sections.heading: Workholding: Clamping and Supporting the Cut
sections.body: More jigsaw problems trace to the workpiece than to the saw. The blade cuts on the upstroke, pulling the work up toward the shoe and dropping it again up to fifty times a second; if the piece can move, it will chatter, the kerf will hammer itself wide, the edge will splinter, and blades will snap. The first principle is therefore rigidity: clamp the work to something heavy, with the cut line overhanging the support by only a modest amount — close enough to the support that the piece cannot flex, far enough that the blade clears the bench. Two clamps beat one, because a single clamp is a pivot. Pad clamp jaws with scrap or cork against finished surfaces. The second principle is managing the offcut. A falling offcut tears a splintered spelch out of the last few centimeters of an otherwise clean cut and can pinch the blade as it sags; support both sides of the line for anything heavy, or have a helper cradle (not pull) the waste, or leave a few millimeters uncut at the end and finish with a handsaw where the piece truly cannot be supported. For long cuts in sheet goods, the elegant solution is to abandon sawhorses-as-bridges entirely and lay the whole sheet flat on a sacrificial bed: a slab of rigid foam insulation 25 to 50 millimeters thick on the floor or across a bench supports the panel continuously on both sides of the kerf, the blade harmlessly scores the foam, nothing sags, nothing pinches, and the cut edge stays clean end to end. The same trick in miniature — a piece of sacrificial hardboard or plywood clamped under the work — both supports thin or flexible stock and nearly eliminates bottom-face breakout, because the fibers at the exit of each tooth are backed by material. Thin sheet metal must be sandwiched top and bottom this way or it will shriek, chatter, and tear. Small workpieces deserve special caution: never hold a small piece in one hand and saw with the other; clamp it, or clamp it inside a larger scrap with a V-notch cut to cradle it. Cutting installed work — countertops, floorboards, door bottoms, wall paneling — inverts the problem: the work is rigid but the surroundings are vulnerable, so check what the blade will meet below (pipes, cables, joists), choose blade length so the stroke's bottom clears anything critical, and where a floorboard must be cut over empty joist space, angle a shallow-set circular saw or use a short blade and keep the shoe flat. Finally, sawing generates a surprising sideways push in curves as the blade's back bears against the kerf wall; a well-clamped piece absorbs this invisibly, while a loosely held one skates — which the beginner then corrects with steering, compounding wander. Rigid work, supported offcut, clear underside: with those three conditions met, an inexpensive saw cuts like an expensive one.

sections.heading: Layout: Marking Curves That Deserve to Be Cut
sections.body: A cut can only be as good as its line, and curve layout is a small craft of its own. For circles and arcs, the compass family does the work: a pencil compass to about 150 millimeters radius, and beyond that a trammel — any rigid strip with a nail or awl through one end as the pivot and a pencil through a hole at the radius. A string looped from a center nail to a pencil works at any size but stretches; keep the string taut and the pencil vertical, and accept that a wooden trammel is more faithful. Mark the center on tape if the surface must stay unmarred. For ellipses, the gardener's method — two pins at the foci with a slack string loop around them and the pencil — draws a true ellipse once the foci are found (each focus lies along the long axis at a distance from the center equal to the square root of half-the-long-axis squared minus half-the-short-axis squared); for a quick approximation, many workers simply trace a large round object of pleasing size. Free curves — the sweep of a shelf bracket, the fair line of a boat frame or a garden-bed edge — are drawn with a batten: a thin, straight-grained strip of wood or a length of PVC trim bent through the points the curve must pass, held by clamps, nails, or a helper's fingers, and traced. The batten's own stiffness distributes curvature evenly and produces what boatbuilders call a fair curve, one with no sudden changes the eye or the saw will stumble over; sight along any drawn curve from a low angle and unfair bumps jump out for correction before cutting. Repeated or precious shapes deserve a template: draw and cut the shape once in hardboard or 6-millimeter MDF, refine it with files and sandpaper until perfect, then trace around it for every copy — and if perfection matters, jigsaw each copy a couple of millimeters outside the traced line and finish with a router and flush-trim bearing bit running on the template, which yields identical, polished edges the jigsaw alone cannot. Scribing fits a workpiece to an irregular surface such as a wavy wall: set a compass to the widest gap between wall and piece, ride the point down the wall while the pencil transfers every bump onto the piece, and cut to the scribed line with a slight back-bevel so the visible edge touches first. Practical marking matters as much as geometry: use a sharp pencil (a knife line for veneered faces, since the severed fibers then release cleanly), mark on masking tape on dark, rough, or melamine surfaces where graphite vanishes, and always mark the waste side with hatching — half the ruined workpieces in the world were cut accurately on the wrong side of a correct line. Decide the blade's relationship to the line before starting: cut just on the waste side, leaving the line intact, so the final dimension survives sanding. The line is a contract; layout is where the job is really decided.

sections.heading: Straight and Guided Cuts
sections.body: Curves are the jigsaw's specialty, but every project mixes in straight cuts, and they expose the tool's flexible-blade nature most cruelly, so technique matters. Freehand, the method is the same relaxed discipline as steering a car: stand or kneel so the forearm can travel the full cut without re-planting, grip lightly, keep the shoe flat and fully on the work, look at the line a few centimeters ahead of the blade rather than at the blade itself, and feed only as fast as the blade cuts willingly. Forcing is the cardinal sin — push harder than the teeth can chew and the flexible blade bows backward and sideways, the cut bellies out of square in the thickness (perfect on top, drifting below), and the extra friction burns the edge. If the saw slows or the motor labors, ease off; if the cut still crawls, the blade is wrong or dull, and no amount of muscle fixes either. A blade that constantly pulls to one side has uneven set or a bent body and belongs in the bin. For long straight cuts, guides remove steering entirely. The manufacturer's rip fence, a T-shaped rod through the shoe, rides a factory edge at up to 20 centimeters or so. Better and more general is a clamped straightedge — a spirit level, a factory plywood strip, or a purpose-made guide rail — set back from the line by the offset between the blade and the edge of the shoe. Measure that offset once with a rule (blade side to shoe edge, typically 35 to 40 millimeters, and note it is different on each side of the shoe), mark it on the saw, and clamping guides becomes a thirty-second habit; keep the shoe pressed lightly against the guide throughout, since drifting away ruins the cut as surely as no guide at all. Some shoes accept adapters for circular-saw guide-rail systems, worth using if already owned. Even guided, a jigsaw's long straight cut in thick stock will show slight under-bevel where the free blade end lags in dense grain; where a dead-square thick edge matters, cut a millimeter or two proud and plane or rout to the line, or use a circular saw for the straights and reserve the jigsaw for the curves — using each tool for its strength is not defeat but craft. Circles deserve a mention here because they are straight-line cutting's rotary cousin: the same rip-fence rod on most saws converts to a circle-cutting trammel with a pivot point, swinging the saw around a center pin for wheels, speaker holes, and round tabletops up to the rod's reach; start the cut from a drilled hole inside the waste, spiral gently out to the circumference, then let the trammel take over. Cut a test circle in scrap first — pivot play shows up as a visible lump where the cut closes on its start.

sections.heading: Cutting Curves: Steering, Feed, and Reading the Blade
sections.body: Curve cutting is a conversation between hands and blade, and the grammar can be stated plainly. Set zero orbit — orbital action widens the effective kerf front-to-back and makes the blade fight turns — and choose the narrowest blade the material allows: a standard wood blade sweeps gentle curves happily, but tight work wants a scroll blade, whose narrowed body turns in roughly half the radius. Position the body so the whole curve can be cut in one flowing pass without re-gripping; where that is impossible, plan pause points on the gentlest parts of the line, never mid-turn. Start the saw at full speed, enter the cut, and steer the way a boat is steered: the saw rotates around the blade, so turning is a smooth swing of the tool's tail while the blade itself advances along the line, and the shoe stays flat and planted through every degree of the turn. The two beginner errors are opposites of each other. The first is steering with side pressure — pushing the blade sideways toward the line like a pencil — which flexes the free bottom end of the blade so the top of the cut follows the line while the bottom undercuts wide; the cut looks right until the pieces separate and the edge is beveled and bellied. The correction is always rotation, never lateral push. The second is feeding too fast for the turn: a blade can only remove so much material per stroke, and in a curve it must remove extra from the kerf's outer wall; rushing makes the blade twist, wander, and overheat. Slow the feed in the turns and let the speed live in the straights, exactly like driving. Watch the line, not the blade — specifically, watch where the line disappears under the front of the shoe a few centimeters ahead, and keep the sawdust blown or extracted off it, because a steering correction made late is a visible flat spot on the finished curve. If the blade begins to sing, smoke, or lag, retreat: back the saw up a few millimeters within the kerf while running (never while stopped, and never yank a stalled blade sideways out of a cut), then resume at a gentler feed. When a cut must change direction sharply and the radius is beyond the blade's ability, do not force the turn; run out into the waste, loop around, and come back at the line from the new direction, or use relief cuts. Two habits produce visibly better curves immediately. First, cut fractionally on the waste side and treat the last half millimeter as sanding allowance — a curve smoothed with a sanding block, drum, or spokeshave forgives every tiny wobble the saw left. Second, practice the specific curve on scrap of the same material for thirty seconds; hands learn a radius astonishingly fast, and the scrap teaches the exact feed rate at which this blade in this wood cuts sweetly. Fluency at curves is nothing more than these rules made automatic.

sections.heading: Tight Radii, Relief Cuts, and Sharp Corners
sections.body: Every blade has a minimum turning radius set by its width from tooth tip to back edge — force a tighter turn and the blade twists in the kerf, binds, burns, and either wanders off line or snaps. A standard wood blade around 7 to 8 millimeters wide turns comfortably down to roughly 25 to 40 millimeters of radius; a scroll blade around 4 millimeters wide manages 10 to 15; nothing hand-held turns a true zero. The craft lies in strategies that make tight geometry cuttable anyway. Relief cuts are the master technique for tight outside curves: before cutting the curve itself, make a series of straight cuts from the waste edge inward, stopping just shy of the line, spaced a couple of centimeters apart around the tight section. As the curve cut then proceeds, each waste segment falls away in turn, the kerf stays open behind the blade, and the blade negotiates the curve as a series of gentle arcs instead of one impossible turn. The tighter the radius, the closer the relief cuts. For tight inside curves, drill instead: bore a hole with a twist or Forstner bit whose radius equals the desired corner radius, placed tangent to both lines inside the waste, then saw along each line into the hole — the drilled arc becomes the finished corner, cleaner than any steered turn, and a row of such holes can pre-form an entire serpentine line. For sharp interior corners, as in a rectangular cutout, the honest geometry is that a round blade path cannot produce a square inside corner directly; the standard sequence is to saw the first side past the corner slightly into the waste, loop out through the waste and back to cut the second side cleanly into the corner, then return to nibble out the remaining fillet with the blade's front teeth, or simply finish the last few millimeters of each corner with a handsaw, chisel, or rasp. Where the corner will be visible and crisp matters, drill a small hole at each corner first (inside the waste, tangent to both lines), saw hole to hole, and square the corners by hand — and remember that in many materials a small radiused corner is structurally better than a sharp one, because square inside corners concentrate stress and start cracks, which is why aircraft windows are round; specify a radius wherever the design allows. On-the-spot direction changes have a technique of their own: to turn the saw around inside a cut without a loop, cut forward, back the blade up a couple of centimeters, and re-cut while swinging gently, widening the kerf enough locally for the blade to rotate — slower than looping through waste, but invaluable when the waste is not expendable. Finally, spiral-toothed scroll blades that cut in any direction exist for extreme pattern work, at real cost in edge quality and control; for most users, relief cuts, drilled corners, and waste loops cover everything a pattern can demand.

sections.heading: Interior Cutouts: Sink Openings, Slots, and Windows
sections.body: The interior cutout — a hole that starts and ends inside a panel, touching no edge — is the jigsaw's defining job, and the sink opening in a kitchen worktop is its classic exam. The universal method is the drilled starter hole: bore 10 to 12 millimeter holes in the waste, snug against but not touching the line, drop the blade in, and saw away; a hole near each corner of a rectangular opening means the corners nearly cut themselves. The alternative is the plunge cut, for experienced hands only: with a short, stiff blade at zero orbit, tip the saw forward onto the front edge of its shoe over open waste, start at full speed, and pivot slowly down so the moving teeth mill their own entry slot until the shoe lies flat. It saves drilling in soft sheet materials and goes wrong suddenly if rushed — practicing on scrap, or simply drilling, is never wrong. For a sink or hob, lay out from the manufacturer's template or the measured rim: the cut line falls inside the rim by the specified flange width (commonly around 10 millimeters), corners get their radius, and everything is checked against the actual appliance and the cabinet below — including rails, pipes, and cables in the blade's path. Laminate tops chip: use a reverse-tooth blade from above, or tape and knife-score the line. What ruins most openings is the unsupported waste, which sags near the end, pinches the blade, and tears the final corner — so support it before the last side. The numbered procedure below is worth following literally the first several times; slots and windows in paneling follow the same logic scaled down, with one addition for walls: check behind with a stud finder and live-wire detector before cutting any surface you cannot see behind.
steps: Mark the opening from the template or the measured appliance rim, checking the flange overlap on all sides and the clearance inside the cabinet below.
Confirm the underside of the cut path is clear of rails, pipes, and cables, and set blade length so the stroke bottom clears anything close.
Tape the line on laminate or veneer, re-mark on the tape, and score the surface layer with a sharp knife.
Drill a 10-12 mm starter hole in the waste near each corner, just clear of the line, keeping the drill vertical.
Fit the right blade (reverse-tooth for laminate from above, fine ground for veneer), set zero orbit and medium speed, and fit the anti-splinter insert.
Insert the blade in a starter hole, let it reach full speed, and cut each side just on the waste side of the line, corner hole to corner hole.
Before cutting the final side, support the waste: screw a batten across it onto the waste, or station a helper below to cradle it without pulling.
Complete the final side at a gentle feed, lift out the waste, and finish corners to their radius with a rasp or sanding drum.
Test-fit the appliance, ease the opening where it binds, then seal exposed chipboard or wood edges (silicone or sealer) before final installation.

sections.heading: Bevel Cuts and Cutting at an Angle
sections.body: Every jigsaw shoe tilts, and the bevel capability is more useful than most owners realize, but it obeys stricter physics than square cutting. Mechanically, a lever or a hex-key screw releases the shoe, which pivots to detents commonly at 15, 30, and 45 degrees and locks anywhere between; detents are convenient but not gospel, so for work that matters, set the angle with a protractor or a sliding bevel against the blade itself, and cut a test piece — shoe scales on inexpensive saws are routinely a degree or two off, and a degree matters when two beveled edges must meet. The uses are everywhere once noticed. A 45-degree bevel lets skirting boards, trim, and boxes meet at mitered corners. A slight back-bevel of 3 to 5 degrees is the secret of scribed fitting: when a cabinet side or worktop is scribed to a wavy wall, back-beveling the cut means only the visible top edge touches the wall, so it can be eased with a plane or sander to a perfect line without removing material across the whole thickness. Beveled curves — a rounded worktop end with an under-bevel, a decorative arch with a chamfered face — are a jigsaw specialty no circular saw can copy. The physics that changes with tilt: the blade now crosses the material diagonally, so the effective thickness it must cut grows (at 45 degrees, by a factor of about 1.4), feed must slow accordingly, and blade length must be rechecked, since a blade that cleared the work square may bottom out or leave teeth buried on the diagonal. The flexible blade's tendency to deflect grows too — cutting force now has a component pulling the shoe sideways across the work — so bevel cuts want a firm grip on the shoe, zero or low orbit, a stiffer, wider blade than the same cut square, and ideally a clamped guide for straight bevels, because correcting a wandering bevel mid-cut is nearly impossible without leaving a visible step. Splinter behavior shifts as well: the acute-angle face of the cut (the undercut side) is delicate and prone to breakout, so orient the work to put the acute edge where it will be hidden, or tape and score it. Compound situations — a bevel along a curve — are cut exactly like any curve but slower still, and it pays to rehearse on scrap because the visual alignment of blade to line changes with tilt and the eye needs a minute to recalibrate. Two cautions complete the picture: always re-square and verify the shoe at zero afterward, since a shoe left at two degrees quietly ruins the next week of square cuts, and never tilt so far that the blade's stroke can strike the shoe or the roller — check by hand-cycling with the tool unplugged after any large angle change.

sections.heading: Beyond Wood: Metal, Plastics, Laminate, and Tile
sections.body: The jigsaw's second career as a universal sheet-cutting tool depends entirely on respecting each material's failure mode. Metal fails by heat and vibration. In steel sheet — brackets, panels, auto bodywork up to roughly 3 millimeters — use a 21 to 24 TPI bi-metal blade, the lowest speed the saw offers, zero orbit, and lubrication: proper cutting oil, or the workshop standby of rubbing a wax candle along the blade, renewed as it cuts. Progress is measured in millimeters per second, the swarf and the work get genuinely hot (gloves for handling afterward, and keep sawdust cleared away since hot chips can smolder in it), and the reward for patience is a controlled curve in steel that tin snips would distort. Thicker steel, above about 5 or 6 millimeters, is technically possible with the right blade and endless patience but is honestly better work for an angle grinder, bandsaw, or reciprocating saw. Aluminum and other non-ferrous metals cut faster with a slightly coarser metal blade around 12 to 17 TPI, but aluminum's soft chips weld into the gullets — lubricate generously and clear the blade often. All thin sheet under about a millimeter demands the sandwich: clamp it between two pieces of scrap plywood or hardboard and cut the whole stack, which keeps three teeth engaged, silences the chatter, and leaves both faces clean. Plastics fail by heat in a different way: acrylic melts around 160 degrees Celsius and either welds itself shut behind the blade or, cut too aggressively, cracks and chips; polycarbonate is tougher but gums. Use a fine or plastic-rated blade, low speed, zero orbit, light feed, leave any protective film on, back the cut with scrap, and if the kerf re-fuses, slow the stroke rate further — melted-shut cuts are a speed problem, never a blade-sharpness problem. PVC, ABS, and composite decking cut like agreeable softwood at low-to-medium speed. Laminates and melamine-faced boards fail by chipping at the brittle surface: the full defensive stack is a clean-cut or reverse-tooth blade, zero orbit, taped and knife-scored line, anti-splinter insert, and the good face oriented away from the tooth exit (down for standard blades, up for reverse-tooth). Ceramic wall tile — the softer, red- or white-bodied kind — cuts on a carbide-grit blade at low speed with water sponged into the kerf, enabling the curved cuts around pipes and toilet flanges that tile nippers butcher; dense porcelain and stone defeat the method and belong to diamond blades in a wet saw or grinder. Fiber-cement board cuts with dedicated carbide blades but liberates crystalline silica dust, a serious lung hazard: cut outdoors with extraction and a properly fitted P2/N95 or better respirator, or score-and-snap instead. Plaster, drywall, and insulation boards cut easily with coarse blades but reward a knife-and-snap where straightness suffices. In every material the diagnostic loop is identical: listen and watch — squeal means speed or pressure, chatter means support, smoke means blade or feed — and change the variable, not the effort.

sections.heading: From Saw Cut to Finished Edge
sections.body: A jigsaw cut is a beginning, and the difference between amateur and professional work is mostly what happens in the ten minutes after the saw stops. Plan for finishing before cutting: stay a hair on the waste side of the line, leaving half a millimeter to a millimeter of material as a fairing allowance, because it is easy to remove wood and impossible to reattach it. For convex curves, a sanding block wrapped in 80- then 120- then 180-grit paper, worked along (not across) the curve with long strokes, erases saw marks and small wobbles together; keep the block moving through the whole sweep so no one spot dishes. Concave curves want a round form — a sanding drum in a drill or drill press is the fast answer, and a dowel or a spray can wrapped in abrasive is the manual one; match the form's radius to or below the curve's so it rides the surface fairly. Rasps and files bridge saw and abrasive where more than a millimeter must go: a half-round rasp hogs wood quickly (cutting on the push stroke, lifted on the return), a file refines, and the modern milled-tooth rasps cut fast and clog little. A spokeshave — the curve specialist's plane — produces the fairest edges of all in skilled hands, reading the grain and shaving downhill. Check fairness by eye and hand constantly: sight along the curve from a low angle for lumps, and run fingertips along it — skin detects a 0.1-millimeter step that eyes miss. For edges that must be perfect or repeated, the router and flush-trim bearing bit remain the gold standard: fix the refined template to the work, let the bearing ride the template, and the bit machines the sawn edge into an exact copy, glassy and identical every time; climb-cut gingerly where grain tears. Square the arrises (the corners between edge and face) intentionally — a light chamfer or a pass of 120-grit at 45 degrees prevents splintering in use and looks deliberate. Tearout repair, when prevention failed: shallow top-face splinters usually vanish into a small chamfer or roundover; deeper chips glue back if the splinter survived (CA glue, tape clamp, sand flush) or fill with matching wood filler under paint. Sealed edges matter in kitchens and baths — chipboard and MDF drink water through cut edges and swell irreversibly, so any cutout near moisture gets its raw edge coated with silicone, PVA sealer, or paint before installation, including the hidden sink opening no one will ever see again. Metal edges deburr with a file stroke at 45 degrees each face and a quick pass of emery; plastics wet-sand through grits and, for acrylic, flame-polish or buff to clarity. The habit that binds all of this: inspect the edge in raking light before calling any job done, because raking light is how everyone else will eventually see it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting: Wander, Bevel Drift, Tearout, Burning, and Breakage
sections.body: Jigsaw faults are few, recurring, and diagnosable, and each has a mechanism worth knowing because the fix follows from it. Cut wanders off line horizontally: either the blade is dull or unevenly set (one side's teeth sharper than the other's pulls the cut sideways — replace it; blades are consumables and a fresh one solves more mysteries than any technique), the feed is too fast for the material, or the operator is steering with side pressure instead of rotation. Cut square on top but beveled or bellied below — the classic hidden fault, discovered only when the pieces part: the flexible blade's free end deflected, from forcing the feed, from a blade too light for the thickness, from a worn guide roller no longer backing the blade, or from turning tighter than the blade's radius so it twisted in the kerf. Fix with a wider, stiffer, sharp blade, slower feed, orbit reduced, roller inspected, and radii respected. Top-face splintering: inherent to up-cutting teeth in veneered or brittle faces; the defensive stack is a fine or reverse-tooth blade, zero orbit, taped and knife-scored line, anti-splinter insert, good face down for standard blades, and slower feed — any one helps, together they nearly eliminate it. Bottom-face breakout instead: back the work with sacrificial scrap. Burning and smoking: the blade is rubbing more than cutting — dull teeth, clogged gullets (too fine a TPI for thick resinous stock), speed too high in a heat-sensitive material, or a pause with the blade spinning in one spot; in a curve, burning localizes exactly where the radius was forced. Blade breakage has three signatures: snapped at the shank means vibration and a loose or bouncing shoe (plant the shoe, clamp the work); snapped mid-body means twisting in a too-tight turn or levering the saw sideways to correct a wander; teeth stripped in a patch means the material won or the pitch was wrong — hitting a hidden screw, or cutting metal with a wood blade. A blade pulled hot from a long cut and instantly plunged into the next warps; let blades cool. Saw judders violently and the cut hammers: fewer than three teeth engaged (pitch too coarse for thin stock — go finer or sandwich the work), or the blade is bottoming out on a support beneath. Motor labors and progress stalls: the kerf is pinching because the offcut sags — support it — or the blade is buried in material beyond its capacity; in deep cuts, retreat a few millimeters periodically to let chips clear. Excessive vibration at the handle with no cut in progress points to a bent blade or a worn plunger bearing; try a new blade first. And the meta-rule that covers the rest: when a cut goes wrong, stop, back out along the kerf, and diagnose — blade, speed, orbit, support, feed, in that order — because continuing a failing cut converts a small blemish into scrap, and every one of these faults costs less to fix at the moment it first appears than one centimeter later.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Blade Economy, and Choosing a Saw
sections.body: A jigsaw asks little care but repays what it gets. After dusty sessions, unplug it and blow or brush debris from the blade clamp, the roller, and the motor vents — packed dust is the usual reason a tool-less clamp stops clicking home, and blocked vents cook motors. Put a drop of light machine oil on the guide roller's pivot occasionally, and inspect the roller's groove: a deep worn channel means the roller has stopped supporting the blade and needs replacement, an inexpensive part on most brands. Check the shoe for burrs (file them off before they scratch a workpiece), verify its squareness to the blade with a small square after any knock or bevel session, and keep the anti-splinter inserts — they are consumables, cheap in packs. On corded saws, inspect the cable where it enters the body, the classic failure point; on cordless, store batteries part-charged and out of frost. Brushed motors eventually need new carbon brushes — sparking and intermittent power are the symptoms, and brushes are a user-replaceable part on most models. Blade economy deserves deliberate policy rather than habit: blades are the cheapest component of every job and the cause of most bad ones, so buy the good ones (bi-metal for anything repeated, ground-tooth for anything visible), buy them in the multi-packs that halve the unit price, sort them in a labeled case rather than a loose drawer that dulls and bends them, and discard without ceremony any blade that is bent, blued from heat, or noticeably slower than new — sharpening jigsaw blades is not economic. A dedicated blade for metal and another for wood, never interchanged, keeps both honest. When choosing or upgrading a saw, rank the features by what actually changes outcomes: low vibration and a solid, slop-free blade guide come first, because they are the difference between a saw that tracks and one that buzzes; then variable speed with electronics that hold speed under load; then orbital settings; then a shoe that locks positively square and adjusts without hunting for a separate key. Stroke length matters for thick stock, and a barrel grip suits low, close curve work while a top handle suits general use — hold both before deciding. Beyond that, an LED, a blower, tool-less shoe tilt, and rail compatibility are conveniences worth having but not paying much for, and raw wattage is nearly irrelevant within the normal range, since technique and blade dominate cutting speed. Corded saws are lighter for their power and never fade mid-job; cordless saws of the current generation cut everything a household asks and add the freedom that makes the jigsaw's go-anywhere character complete — the choice is logistics, not capability. Treated this way, a mid-priced jigsaw is a decades-long tool: the motor outlives fashions, the consumables stay cheap, and the skills — reading a blade, steering a fair curve, opening a clean hole in the middle of a panel — only compound.

guides.safetyNote: Unplug the saw or remove its battery before every blade change or adjustment. Wear safety glasses (chips fly upward toward the face), keep hands and the cord out of the blade path below the work, and check behind installed surfaces for pipes and cables before cutting. Clamp small workpieces rather than hand-holding them, let the blade stop before withdrawing it, and use a fitted respirator plus extraction for MDF and especially fiber-cement dust, which contains crystalline silica.

guides.title: Reciprocating Saws for Demolition Work
guides.summary: A complete practical guide to using a reciprocating saw for demolition and strip-out work, covering how the tool works, how to choose blades for wood, nail-embedded timber, metal and masonry, correct cutting technique, and the hazards of cutting blind into a building.

sections.heading: What a Reciprocating Saw Is and Why Demolition Belongs to It
sections.body:
A reciprocating saw is a handheld power saw in which a single straight blade, clamped at one end and unsupported at the other, is driven rapidly back and forth along its own axis. The action is essentially that of a hand hacksaw or a keyhole saw performed by a motor a few thousand times a minute. Milwaukee introduced the archetype in 1951 under the trade name Sawzall, which has become the common generic term in North America in the way that Hoover did for vacuum cleaners; in Britain and much of Europe the tool is simply called a reciprocating saw, and compact single-handed versions carry various manufacturers' names.

What makes the tool dominant in demolition and strip-out work is precisely what makes it poor at carpentry: the blade is supported at one end only, is comparatively narrow, and can be swapped in seconds for one suited to a completely different material. That cantilevered blade will reach into a stud bay, around a corner, up inside a ceiling void, behind a pipe run, and through the back of a joist you cannot see. It cuts wood, nails, screws, steel pipe, copper, cast iron, plaster, plastic, roofing felt and fibreglass without changing tools, only blades. Nothing else in the general toolkit combines that reach with that material range. A circular saw is faster and far more accurate in clean timber, but it cannot cut into a wall, it will not tolerate embedded nails, and its blade depth is fixed by geometry.

The price of that versatility is control. The cut is rough, wanders unless you manage it, and the tool shakes hard in the hands. Because the blade is longer than the material is thick, you are frequently cutting blind: a 300 millimetre blade passing through 20 millimetres of plasterboard has 280 millimetres of unsighted travel behind the wall where a cable, a gas pipe or a water main may sit. Almost every serious injury and expensive mistake associated with these saws comes from that single fact, and the whole discipline of using one well is really the discipline of knowing what is on the other side.

The tool's typical jobs are therefore destructive rather than constructive. Cutting out a window frame or door lining flush to the brickwork. Sectioning studwork and joists during a strip-out. Removing old cast-iron or steel waste pipe. Cutting nails and screws in the joint between two components that must be separated without damaging one of them. Pruning tree limbs with a coarse blade. Cutting seized bolts, reinforcing bar, threaded rod and exhaust systems. It is a tool for making things come apart, and for that it has no rival at anything like its cost or size.

sections.heading: How the Tool Works: Drive Mechanism, Stroke and Orbital Action
sections.body:
A universal or brushless motor spins far too fast and with far too little torque to drive a blade directly, so a reduction gearbox trades speed for force and a conversion mechanism turns rotation into linear travel. Most saws use a scotch yoke or a crank and connecting rod, in which an eccentric pin on the output gear runs in a slot in the plunger so that one revolution produces one full forward and back stroke; some premium tools use a wobble-plate drive in which an angled plate nods back and forth against the plunger. In every case the plunger must be stopped dead and thrown the other way several thousand times a minute, and that reversal is where the tool's characteristic violence comes from. Manufacturers fight it with counterweights driven from the same gear, moving opposite to the plunger so the two momenta partly cancel, and better tools add spring-isolated handles. Measured vibration at the handle can differ by a factor of two between models of identical stated power, which translates directly into how many minutes a day you can safely hold the trigger.

Three specifications describe how the tool cuts. Stroke length is the distance the blade travels each pass: lighter saws use around 19 millimetres, three-quarters of an inch, while demolition-class tools use 28.5 or 32 millimetres, an inch and an eighth or an inch and a quarter. Material removal per stroke is proportional to stroke length, so a long-stroke tool cuts substantially faster, and it also spreads the work across more teeth so each tooth spends longer out of the cut shedding heat and chips. Blade life improves markedly as a result.

Stroke rate is quoted in strokes per minute, typically zero to about 3,000 through a variable-speed trigger. It must be matched to the material. Wood rewards full speed. Metal does not: the cutting edge of a high-speed steel tooth begins to soften above roughly 600 degrees Celsius, and heat generation climbs steeply with speed, so a bi-metal blade run flat out in steel will blue and dull within seconds. Use full speed in timber and plastics, half to two-thirds in thick steel, and a slow deliberate rate in thin-walled tube where teeth snatch.

Orbital action, offered on most demolition saws, adds a vertical component so the blade tip traces a shallow ellipse, biting downward on the cutting stroke and lifting on the return. In wood it often increases cutting rate by half again or more, at the cost of a rougher cut and a tool that bucks harder. It must be switched off for metal, where it drives teeth into the work at the wrong angle and strips or snaps them, and off for plunge cuts and any work where control matters more than speed.

sections.heading: Corded, Cordless and Pneumatic: Choosing the Power Source
sections.body:
Corded reciprocating saws are rated in amperes or watts, and demolition-class tools sit between roughly 7.5 and 15 amperes on a 120 volt supply, or about 900 to 1,500 watts on 230 volts. The defining characteristic of a corded tool is that it does not fade. A saw that is halfway through a cast-iron soil stack will hold its stroke rate under load until the job is done, and will do it again all afternoon. For sustained heavy cutting, particularly thick metal, corded remains the more capable choice and the cheaper one for equivalent output. The costs are obvious: a trailing lead in a demolition space is a trip hazard and a cutting hazard, and there is a real and recurring accident category of operators cutting through their own supply cable. Running the lead over your shoulder and away behind you is the standard mitigation, along with a residual current device or ground fault interrupter on the supply, which should be treated as mandatory on any site with water, metal and damaged wiring in the same room.

Cordless tools have improved to the point that they now dominate general demolition use. An 18 or 20 volt platform with a high-capacity lithium-ion pack, typically five to twelve ampere-hours, will cut framing timber, nail-embedded stock and light metal all day given spare batteries, and higher-voltage platforms at 36 to 60 volts close most of the remaining gap. Brushless motors matter here more than anywhere: eliminating the friction and electrical losses of carbon brushes typically yields thirty to fifty percent more work per charge, less heat, and a motor life measured in years rather than a wear part that must be replaced. The real cordless advantage in strip-out work is not convenience but the ability to work up a ladder, inside a ceiling void, or in a building with the power isolated, which is exactly the condition you want the building to be in.

Battery temperature is the practical constraint people underestimate. Heavy cutting draws very high current, cells heat, and protection electronics will cut the tool out to prevent damage. A pack that has just shut down should be swapped rather than coaxed, and packs should not be charged straight off a hard cut. In cold conditions the opposite applies: lithium cells deliver noticeably less below about five degrees Celsius, so packs kept in a warm vehicle outperform packs left in a van overnight.

Pneumatic reciprocating saws exist and are common in vehicle bodyshops, aviation and some heavy industry. They are light, compact, tolerate being dropped and submerged, and cannot start an electrical fire, which matters in fuel-contaminated or explosive atmospheres. Their limitation is that they need a substantial compressor, generally several cubic feet per minute at ninety pounds per square inch, which makes them impractical for occasional building work. A related family, hydraulic saws, is used by fire and rescue services for exactly the same reasons at much higher power.

sections.heading: Blade Metallurgy: What Blades Are Made Of and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Blade choice determines cutting performance far more than the tool does. A good saw with the wrong blade is useless; a mediocre saw with the right blade will finish the job. The blade market divides first by material, and the differences are metallurgical rather than cosmetic.

High carbon steel, usually abbreviated HCS, is a plain hardened carbon steel throughout. It is cheap and very flexible, which means it bends rather than snaps and is forgiving of a wandering cut. It is also soft: its teeth lose their edge quickly and it will not survive contact with a nail. HCS blades are for clean softwood, plastic and pruning, and nothing else. High-speed steel, or HSS, is alloyed with tungsten, molybdenum, chromium and vanadium and retains hardness at temperatures that would ruin carbon steel, which is what allows it to cut metal. Its weakness is brittleness. An all-HSS blade in a tool that shakes and twists will fracture, often in the first minute, and it is now rarely sold for general use.

The workhorse of the trade is the bi-metal blade, usually marked BIM. A narrow strip of high-speed steel is electron-beam or laser welded along the toothed edge of a flexible spring-steel body, and the teeth are then cut and hardened. The result is a blade with HSS cutting edges and a body that flexes rather than shattering, and it will typically outlast an HCS blade by a factor of ten in mixed material while surviving the incidental nail strikes that define demolition work. Any general demolition blade you buy should be bi-metal unless you have a specific reason to choose otherwise.

Above bi-metal sit two carbide families. Carbide-tipped blades have individual tungsten carbide teeth brazed to a steel body. Carbide is far harder than HSS and holds an edge at higher temperature, so these blades cut stainless steel, hardened fasteners, cast iron, reinforcing bar and abrasive nail-embedded timber where bi-metal simply wears away, and manufacturers commonly claim twenty to fifty times the life in such material. They cost several times as much and are brittle in a different way: a carbide tooth will chip if the blade is allowed to chatter or if the tip strikes the work at speed, so they must be started gently. Carbide-grit blades have no teeth at all; tungsten carbide particles are bonded to a continuous edge, and they abrade rather than cut. That makes them the answer for cast-iron pipe, ceramic tile, fibre cement, brick, fibreglass, plaster with embedded lath and other materials that would strip a toothed blade instantly. Diamond-grit versions extend the same principle to harder stone and porcelain, at slow cutting rates.

sections.heading: Tooth Geometry, Pitch and Matching Blade to Material
sections.body:
Beyond the blade's material, the geometry of its teeth determines what it can cut and how fast. The primary specification is pitch, expressed in the English-speaking trades as teeth per inch, or TPI, and occasionally as tooth spacing in millimetres. Coarse blades in the range of three to six teeth per inch have large gullets, the valleys between teeth that carry chips out of the kerf, and cut fast and roughly in wood. Around six to ten teeth per inch is the general demolition range for nail-embedded timber, coarse enough to be quick and fine enough to survive metal. Ten to fourteen suits general-purpose metal and thicker sections. Fourteen to eighteen is for structural steel and heavier plate. Eighteen to twenty-four is for thin material: electrical conduit, sheet metal, thin-wall tube and small-diameter copper.

The rule that governs the choice is simple and worth memorising: at least three teeth must be in contact with the material at all times. If the material is thinner than the tooth spacing, individual teeth drop into the gap and then catch on the far edge, which snatches the blade, strips teeth and can throw the saw. This is why cutting a millimetre-wall copper tube with a six-teeth-per-inch demolition blade destroys both the blade and the tube, and why the same blade goes through a joist without complaint. To check quickly, divide 25.4 millimetres by the tooth count to get the spacing and confirm that the material thickness is at least three times that figure.

Two refinements appear on better blades. Variable pitch means tooth spacing changes along the blade, typically from coarse near the tip to finer near the shank, or in a repeating pattern. This breaks up the resonance that produces the characteristic howl and chatter of a constant-pitch blade in metal, reduces vibration, and lets a single blade handle a wider thickness range. Tooth set describes how alternate teeth are bent slightly left and right so that the kerf is wider than the blade body, which stops the blade binding in its own cut. Coarse wood blades use a wide raker set; fine metal blades use a subtle wavy set in which teeth are set in gentle groups.

Rake angle, the forward lean of the tooth face, completes the picture. Aggressive positive rake, common on wood and pruning blades, takes a deep bite and pulls the blade into the work. Neutral or slightly negative rake, standard on metal blades, scrapes more than it hooks, generates less grab and survives interrupted cuts. This is why a wood blade in steel not only dulls but snatches dangerously, and why a metal blade in timber feels sluggish even when sharp.

sections.heading: Blade Length, Thickness and Building a Working Blade Kit
sections.body:
Blade length is quoted as overall length including the shank, and the usable cutting length is roughly 25 millimetres less. The governing constraint is that the blade must be long enough that its tip clears the far side of the material at the end of every stroke, otherwise the tip stays buried, chips are never ejected, and the blade overheats and jams. As a working rule, choose a blade at least 40 to 50 millimetres longer than the material is thick. A 150 millimetre blade handles most framing timber and pipe. A 230 millimetre blade covers deep joists and doubled studs. Blades of 300 millimetres and beyond exist for cutting through thick timbers or in from one face of a wall, and they whip and wander badly; treat length beyond what the job requires as a liability rather than a bonus.

Thickness is the specification most people never look at and the one that separates a demolition blade from a general blade. Standard blades are around 0.9 millimetres thick, about 0.035 of an inch. Demolition-rated blades are commonly 1.6 millimetres, around 0.062 of an inch, nearly twice as stiff in the plane that matters. A thick blade resists the twisting that occurs when you pull a partly buried blade sideways, which is the single most common way blades break, and it wanders far less in a long cut. The trade-off is a wider kerf, slower cutting for the same power, and less ability to flex for flush work. Height, the front-to-back dimension of the blade body, has a similar effect: taller blades resist bending but will not follow a curve.

A sensible working kit for building demolition is small. It should contain a stack of 150 millimetre bi-metal blades at six to ten teeth per inch for nail-embedded timber, which will be the bulk of what you consume. Add 230 millimetre versions of the same for deeper cuts. Add fourteen and eighteen teeth per inch bi-metal blades for structural steel and thin metal respectively. Add one or two carbide-tipped blades for stainless, hardened bolts and reinforcing bar. Add one carbide-grit blade for cast iron, tile and fibre cement. Finally add a couple of coarse, aggressive blades at three to five teeth per inch for green wood and roots, since sap and bark clog a fine blade instantly.

Blades are consumables and should be treated as such. A blunt blade does not simply cut slowly; it generates far more heat, requires more feed pressure, vibrates more, wanders more, and is much more likely to snap. The economics are stark: a blade costs a few units of currency and a wasted twenty minutes of labour costs far more, so changing a blade at the first sign that it is not cutting cleanly is always the cheaper decision.

sections.heading: Setting Up: Blade Changes, Shoe Adjustment and Pre-Cut Checks
sections.body:
Preparation is where demolition accidents are prevented, because once the blade is moving you have already committed. The single most important habit is to establish what is behind the surface before cutting into it: electrical cables, gas pipes, water pipes, waste pipes and heating runs. Cables commonly run vertically above and below sockets and switches and horizontally within about 150 millimetres of ceilings and floors, but that is a convention rather than a guarantee and older or amateur work follows no rule at all. A combined metal, wood and live-cable detector is worth its cost many times over, though none is reliable enough to be trusted alone: verify by isolating circuits, by cutting a small inspection opening with a hand tool first, or by looking from the other side.

The shoe, sometimes called the foot, is the flat plate surrounding the blade at the nose of the tool, and using it correctly is the difference between control and chaos. Pressed firmly against the workpiece, it transfers the tool's reciprocating reaction into the material rather than into your arms, which dramatically reduces vibration, chatter and blade breakage. Many saws have an adjustable shoe; extending it moves the cutting action onto a fresh part of a partly worn blade.

The workpiece itself must be considered before the cut, not during it. A section of timber cut free will fall, and it will fall with any weight it carries: plasterboard, insulation, water in a pipe, or the load of a structure above. Establish what is holding what up. Structural members must never be cut without understanding the load path and providing temporary support, and if the answer is uncertain, that is a question for a structural engineer rather than a saw. Used blades stay hot enough to burn for several minutes after cutting stops.
steps: Isolate the tool completely: unplug a corded saw at the wall, or remove the battery from a cordless one.
Rotate the clamp collar or lift the lever, withdraw the old blade, and check it for heat before touching it bare-handed.
Blow or brush sawdust, plaster and metal chips out of the clamp, the usual cause of a blade that will not seat or stay put.
Insert the new blade until the tang bottoms out, teeth-down for normal cuts or teeth-up when cutting close to a floor or overhead.
Release the collar and pull hard on the blade by hand; a blade that moves at all must be reseated.
Set the shoe extension to use a fresh part of the blade, and set orbital action on for wood or off for metal and plunge cuts.
Scan the cut line with a cable and pipe detector, then isolate any circuit that could run through the area at the consumer unit.
Confirm what the piece supports and what will fall when it is severed, and add temporary propping or a second pair of hands.
Fit eye and hearing protection and gloves, clear your footing and the path of falling material, then reconnect power and brace before cutting.

sections.heading: Cutting Technique: Stance, Shoe Pressure and Control
sections.body:
A reciprocating saw is used with two hands wherever the geometry permits: one gripping the rear handle and operating the trigger, the other on the barrel or front grip immediately behind the gearbox. That forward hand does most of the controlling, because it is closest to the cut and has the mechanical advantage to hold the shoe against the work. Stand with feet apart and one foot back, elbows slightly bent rather than locked, and position yourself so that if the saw suddenly frees itself the blade travels into empty space rather than into your leg or your other hand. Never place a supporting hand on the far side of the material within a blade's length of the cut.

The core skill is shoe pressure. Press the shoe firmly and continuously against the workpiece throughout the cut so the tool pivots on it and the reciprocating reaction is fed into the material. When the shoe lifts, the whole tool begins to bounce against the blade's motion, the blade flexes on each stroke, cutting slows, vibration multiplies and the blade fatigues and snaps. Beginners almost universally push the blade harder and hold the shoe more loosely, which is exactly backwards. Feed pressure into the blade should be modest: enough for the teeth to bite, not enough to bow the blade or stall the motor. If the cut is slow, the answer is a sharper or coarser blade, not more force.

Start every cut with the shoe already in contact and the blade just clear of the material, then squeeze the trigger to bring the blade up to speed before advancing it. Starting a stationary blade against the work causes it to skate across the surface, which marks finished work and can wrench the tool sideways. In metal, start slowly and let a groove establish before increasing speed. Where a blade must be started at an awkward angle, filing or hacksawing a small starting notch takes ten seconds and prevents the wander that otherwise ruins the line.

Long cuts require reading the material as it opens. Timber under load will pinch the blade as the kerf closes, which stalls the saw and can snap the blade or throw the tool; watch for the kerf narrowing and relieve it with a wedge or by cutting from the other side. Conversely a kerf opening ahead of the blade means the piece is about to break free early, and the cut should be finished from the far end so the piece drops cleanly. When the blade binds, release the trigger immediately and let the tool stop before attempting to withdraw it; pulling a running blade out of a bind is how blades break and how the saw kicks back into the operator.

sections.heading: Plunge Cuts, Flush Cuts and Awkward Access
sections.body:
Three specialist cuts account for most of what a reciprocating saw does that no other tool can. The first is the plunge cut, starting a cut in the middle of a panel with no edge to enter from. The technique is to rest the front edge of the shoe on the surface with the blade tip angled away and clear, start the saw at moderate speed with the orbital action switched off, and then slowly pivot the tool about the shoe edge so that the blade tip descends into the material under control. The shoe acts as a fulcrum throughout, which is why the manoeuvre must never be attempted with the shoe held off the surface. Plunge cutting is easy in plasterboard and softwood, harder in dense timber, and effectively impossible in metal, where the correct approach is to drill a starter hole. Because the tip descends blind, plunge cutting into a wall or ceiling is the highest-risk operation in the whole repertoire, and the depth reached should be limited deliberately, either by controlling the pivot or by fitting the shortest blade that will do the job.

The second is the flush cut, severing something tight against a surface that must survive: nails between a joist and floorboard, bolts against a wall, a pipe against a slab. Three approaches work. A dedicated flush-cut blade has an offset or cranked shank so its teeth sit in line with the shoe, letting the blade lie flat against the surface. A long thin bi-metal blade can be flexed deliberately, running it with the shoe tilted so the blade bows and its middle contacts the surface, which is effective but hard on blades and requires a light touch. Some tools allow the blade to be mounted sideways at ninety degrees, turning the saw on its side to reach into corners. A scrap of sheet metal or a thin timber offcut slipped between the blade and the surface being protected is a cheap and very effective sacrificial guard.

The third is cutting in genuinely constrained space, which is where compact one-handed saws earn their keep. These use shorter strokes, typically around 19 millimetres, and much smaller bodies, and they will reach inside a stud bay or under a sink where a full-size tool will not. One-handed operation is acceptable on such a tool with light material, but demands that the shoe still be pressed to the work and that the other hand be nowhere near the blade path.

In all three cases the same discipline applies: control comes from the shoe, orbital action stays off, speed is moderate rather than maximum, and the blade is the shortest that will reach through. A very long blade in an awkward cut is a tool with an unpredictable tip, and the tip is the part you cannot see.

sections.heading: Nail-Embedded Timber and Structural Strip-Out
sections.body:
Most demolition cutting is nail-embedded timber, and it is a genuinely distinct material rather than simply wood with something in it. A blade travelling at three thousand strokes per minute meets steel without warning, and the impact is what kills blades and jars operators. Purpose-made demolition blades address this with thicker bodies around 1.6 millimetres, tougher bi-metal construction, a pitch around six to ten teeth per inch that compromises between wood speed and metal survival, and often a reinforced tooth form or carbide tips. Using a clean-wood blade in this work is a false economy measured in minutes.

Technique adapts accordingly. Reduce speed slightly rather than running flat out, keep the shoe hard against the timber, and expect the tool to lurch when the blade finds a nail. Where a nail is visible, it is often better to cut it deliberately with the blade square to it, at a slower rate, than to hit it obliquely at speed and strip a run of teeth. Old cut nails and hardened masonry nails are considerably tougher than modern wire nails, and reclaimed timber may contain screws, plates, staples and the occasional embedded bolt, any of which will stall a blade instantly and twist the tool in your hands if you are leaning into the cut rather than holding the shoe steady against the timber.

In strip-out work the fastest method is usually to cut connections rather than members. To separate a stud partition, running a long blade down the joint between the sole plate and floor, or between stud and plate, cuts the nails and lets the components come apart intact, which is quicker than sawing through timber and leaves reusable material. The same applies to removing a door lining, a window frame or nailed trim: cut the fasteners in the gap rather than destroying the component.

The structural question must be settled before any of this. Loads travel down through a building along a definite path, and cutting a member that is part of that path transfers its load somewhere it may not be able to go. Joists, rafters, purlins, lintels, structural studs in loadbearing walls, and any timber that supports something above it must be identified and, where they are to be cut or removed, temporarily supported with propping designed for the load. The warning signs that a member is loadbearing include running perpendicular to floor joists above, sitting directly under a wall on the floor above, carrying a beam or a purlin, or forming part of a run that continues down through the building to a foundation. Where any doubt exists, stop. A reciprocating saw makes an irreversible cut in about two seconds, and there is no version of this work in which guessing about structure is acceptable.

sections.heading: Cutting Metal: Pipe, Conduit, Bar and Fasteners
sections.body:
Metal cutting is where blade selection and speed control stop being refinements and become the whole job. The mechanism to keep in mind is heat. Each tooth removes a chip, and the energy of that deformation becomes heat concentrated in a very small volume at the cutting edge. High-speed steel begins to soften above roughly 600 degrees Celsius, which a blade run at full speed in steel will reach within seconds. A blade that turns blue has already been ruined; the colour is the oxide film that forms as the steel is tempered back and loses hardness.

The countermeasures are straightforward and dramatically effective. Reduce stroke rate to roughly half to two-thirds of maximum. Switch orbital action off entirely. Apply steady moderate pressure rather than intermittent hard pushes, because a tooth that rubs without cutting generates heat without removing material. Above all, use cutting fluid: a stick of cutting wax, tapping fluid, or in a pinch general purpose oil applied to the cut every twenty or thirty seconds will commonly double or triple blade life and noticeably speed the cut, since it lubricates the chip-tooth interface and carries heat away.

Match pitch to wall thickness with the three-teeth-in-contact rule. Thin-wall electrical conduit, small-bore copper and sheet metal need eighteen to twenty-four teeth per inch. Steel pipe, angle iron and plate from about three to six millimetres take fourteen to eighteen. Solid bar and heavy section take ten to fourteen. Reinforcing bar deserves particular care: it is hard, abrasive and often under tension in concrete, and a carbide-tipped blade at low speed with fluid is far the better tool than a bi-metal blade flogged until it fails. Cast-iron pipe, which is hard and brittle and will strip teeth immediately, calls for a carbide-grit blade, though for larger diameters a snap cutter is faster and safer.

Two hazards are specific to metal. First, the offcut and the swarf are hot and sharp; steel chips thrown from a reciprocating saw will embed in skin and are a leading cause of eye injury, which is why eye protection here means sealed goggles rather than open-sided spectacles. Second, pipe must be assumed to contain something until proven otherwise. Gas pipe must be isolated and, where required by local rules, purged by a competent person before any powered cutting; a spark in a gas-filled void is not survivable. Water pipe should be drained. Steel conduit and armoured cable may still be live, and cutting into a live conductor with an earthed metal blade produces an arc flash at the point of contact. Verify isolation electrically, at the cut, before starting. Pipework under pressure or holding hot water will also spray when it is breached, so drain and vent it before the blade goes in rather than discovering the contents halfway through the cut.

sections.heading: Plaster, Masonry, Plastics and Other Awkward Materials
sections.body:
Beyond timber and metal lies a category of materials that behave badly under a toothed blade, and knowing which is which saves a great deal of frustration. The general principle is that hard brittle materials should be abraded rather than cut, which means a carbide-grit or diamond-grit blade, while soft thermoplastics need coarse teeth and low speed to avoid melting.

Plasterboard cuts effortlessly with almost any blade and produces enormous quantities of fine gypsum dust. Traditional lath and plaster is more difficult: the plaster is hard and abrasive and dulls teeth quickly, while the timber laths splinter, and the combination is best handled with a coarse bi-metal blade accepted as sacrificial, or a carbide-grit blade if the plaster is thick. Fibre cement board, common as soffit and cladding, is highly abrasive and produces respirable crystalline silica; it requires a carbide-grit blade and genuine respiratory protection, and is much better cut with dust extraction or scored and snapped where possible.

Brick, block and mortar can be cut with a carbide-grit blade for small jobs such as removing a single brick or cutting a chase, but this is slow and hard on the tool, and beyond a few cuts an angle grinder with a diamond blade or a proper cut-off saw is the right answer. Ceramic tile cuts reasonably with carbide grit. Concrete containing aggregate will destroy anything a reciprocating saw can hold; the only sensible uses in concrete are cutting exposed reinforcing bar after the concrete has been broken away.

Plastics divide by type. Rigid PVC waste pipe and uPVC frame sections cut cleanly with a fine to medium blade at moderate speed; run too fast and friction melts the plastic, which then welds behind the blade and binds it. Polyethylene and polypropylene are worse in this respect and want a coarse blade at low speed so that chips clear rather than smear. Acrylic and polycarbonate sheet chip and crack easily and are better cut with a fine-toothed blade and firm backing. Glass-reinforced plastic, fibreglass and carbon composite are extremely abrasive: a carbide-grit blade is the correct choice, and the dust from both glass and carbon fibre is a respiratory and skin irritant requiring a respirator and covered arms.

Green wood, roots and branches want the coarsest available blade, three to five teeth per inch, with large gullets and aggressive set, because sap and wet fibre pack a fine blade solid within a few cuts. Pruning blades are made for exactly this. Roots frequently contain embedded grit and small stones, so expect to consume blades and never use a good metal blade underground. Bitumen, roofing felt and insulation board all clog blades and are best cut with coarse teeth at moderate speed, cleaning the blade periodically with a scraper or solvent.

sections.heading: Dust, Contamination and the Hazards Hidden in Old Buildings
sections.body:
Demolition disturbs materials that were stable while intact, and a reciprocating saw at three thousand strokes per minute is an efficient generator of airborne particles. Three contaminants dominate the risk in older buildings, and all three are invisible.

Asbestos was used extensively in construction until it was progressively banned, with the timing varying by country: the United Kingdom banned blue and brown asbestos in 1985 and white asbestos in 1999, while the United States restricted but never comprehensively banned it, so American buildings of many ages may contain it. It appears in insulation board, ceiling tiles, textured coatings, pipe lagging, cement sheet, vinyl floor tile backing, rope seals and countless other products. Power cutting asbestos-containing material releases fibres in quantities that are genuinely dangerous, and the diseases it causes, asbestosis, pleural mesothelioma and lung cancer, have latency periods of twenty to forty years, so nothing about the exposure feels harmful at the time. The correct response to suspected asbestos is to stop, not to work carefully: in most jurisdictions a survey before demolition is a legal requirement and licensed contractors must handle higher-risk materials.

Lead paint is the second. Housing built before 1978 in the United States, and before around 1992 in the United Kingdom, may carry lead-based paint, and cutting or sanding it produces fine lead dust that is absorbed by ingestion and inhalation. Children and pregnant women are most vulnerable, and there is no established safe blood lead level. Contain the area with plastic sheeting, avoid dry sweeping, use a vacuum with a certified high-efficiency filter, wash thoroughly, and do not eat, drink or smoke in the work area.

Respirable crystalline silica is the third and is present wherever concrete, mortar, brick, stone, fibre cement or engineered stone is cut. Particles under about ten micrometres reach the deep lung and cause silicosis, an irreversible fibrotic disease, and increase risks of lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and kidney disease. The United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration set a permissible exposure limit of 50 micrograms per cubic metre averaged over eight hours in its 2016 rule, a level reached quickly by dry cutting in an enclosed space. Control means water suppression where electrically safe, on-tool extraction, ventilation, and a fitted respirator of at least FFP3 or N100 class rather than a nuisance dust mask. A disposable mask that has not been fit-tested and does not seal against the face provides far less protection than most users assume, and beards defeat the seal entirely.

Two habits reduce all three exposures at once. First, separate the work area from the rest of the building with sheeting taped over doorways, and switch off any forced-air heating or ventilation that would otherwise distribute dust through the property. Second, treat clean-up as part of the job rather than an afterthought, because settled dust is re-suspended by every footstep for weeks afterwards. Work clothing should be removed on site and washed separately: carrying lead or asbestos dust home on overalls is a well documented route of secondary exposure to families.

sections.heading: Vibration, Noise, Kickback and Personal Protection
sections.body:
Reciprocating saws are among the most aggressive vibrating tools in general use, and the injury they cause most often is not dramatic but cumulative. Hand-arm vibration syndrome results from prolonged exposure and produces permanent damage to blood vessels, nerves and joints: tingling and numbness in the fingers, loss of grip strength and dexterity, and episodes of painful blanching known as vibration white finger, triggered by cold. The damage does not reverse. Under the United Kingdom's Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005 the daily exposure action value is 2.5 metres per second squared averaged over eight hours and the exposure limit value is 5. Reciprocating saws commonly measure between 10 and 25 metres per second squared, which means the action value can be reached in well under an hour of actual trigger time and the limit value within a couple of hours. Practical control means rotating the task between workers, taking genuine breaks, keeping blades sharp so cuts finish faster, choosing tools with counterbalancing and isolated handles, gripping no more tightly than necessary, and keeping hands warm.

Noise is the parallel exposure. These tools typically produce between 95 and 105 A-weighted decibels at the operator's ear, well above the 85 decibel action level at which hearing protection becomes necessary in most regulatory regimes. Because the decibel scale is logarithmic, every three decibel increase halves the permissible exposure time, so at 100 decibels safe unprotected exposure is measured in minutes. Noise-induced hearing loss is painless, gradual and permanent. Ear defenders or properly inserted plugs should be worn for every cut, not only long ones.

Kickback in a reciprocating saw is different from that of a circular saw but no less sudden. It occurs when the blade binds in the kerf, when the tip catches on something unseen, or when the shoe is not in contact so that the tool's reaction throws it rather than the blade. The result is a violent sideways or backward lurch of a tool with an exposed blade. The defences are keeping the shoe pressed to the work, using both hands, standing so the blade path misses your body, releasing the trigger the instant the tool binds, and never reaching around or behind the material.

Minimum protective equipment is eye protection to a recognised standard such as ANSI Z87.1 or EN 166, preferably sealed goggles when cutting metal because chips arrive from unpredictable directions; hearing protection; gloves that resist cuts and damp vibration without being loose enough to catch; a respirator matched to the dust; and boots with toe protection, because everything you cut free eventually falls. Loose clothing, dangling cords, watches and jewellery must be removed, and long hair tied back.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Troubleshooting and Common Failures
sections.body:
A reciprocating saw has few user-serviceable parts, but a small amount of routine attention prevents most of the failures that take one out of service. Air vents clog with dust and cause overheating, so they should be blown clear regularly with low-pressure compressed air. The blade clamp mechanism accumulates packed debris and should be cleaned and given a trace of light oil; the great majority of blades that will not seat or that fall out mid-cut are held by a dirty clamp rather than a broken one. Brushed motors have carbon brushes that wear and eventually cause sparking, loss of power and intermittent running; they are cheap and often replaceable through external caps, and replacing them at the first sign of trouble prevents commutator damage that ends the tool. Brushless motors remove this maintenance item entirely.

The shoe wears and its pivot loosens with hard use, and a shoe that rattles transmits vibration and lets the tool chatter; replacements are inexpensive. Gearboxes are packed with grease at the factory and rarely need attention, but a saw that begins to whine, run hot at the nose, or lose stroke length should be opened by a service centre rather than run to destruction. Cordless tool contacts should be kept clean, and batteries stored at a partial charge in moderate temperature rather than either fully flat or on charge indefinitely.

Several symptoms have reliable diagnoses. A blade that snaps repeatedly near the shank indicates the shoe is not being held against the work, or that the blade is too thin for the job, or that the tool is being twisted in the cut. Teeth stripping in a run points to too coarse a pitch for the material thickness, or orbital action left on in metal, or striking a hardened fastener. A blade that turns blue means excessive speed with no lubrication. Cutting that has become slow while the blade still looks sharp usually means the teeth are rounded and the blade should be replaced regardless of appearance. A tool that bogs down and smells hot is being over-fed; ease off and let it run.
