Wandering cuts have three causes worth separating: a blade too long or too thin for the depth, so it flexes; a blade dull on one side so it steers; or a bent blade, which must be discarded rather than straightened. Excessive vibration that appeared suddenly usually means a loose blade, a loose shoe, or a blade with missing teeth on one side. Finally, a tool that will not start on a cordless platform is more often a battery in protection shutdown than a failure, and one that trips a residual current device repeatedly should be taken out of service and tested rather than plugged into an unprotected socket.

sections.heading: When the Reciprocating Saw Is the Wrong Tool
sections.body:
The reciprocating saw's versatility invites overuse, and knowing its limits is as valuable as knowing its techniques. It is a rough tool. The cut edge is torn rather than sheared, the line wanders by several millimetres over a long cut even in skilled hands, and the vibration marks any finished surface the shoe rests on. For any cut that will be seen or that must be dimensionally accurate, the wrong tool has been chosen. Straight cuts in sheet material and framing belong to a circular saw or a track saw; curves and fine work belong to a jigsaw or bandsaw; and joinery belongs to a mitre saw or table saw.

For work close to finished surfaces, the oscillating multi-tool is almost always better. Its blade oscillates through a small angle at high frequency and can be placed precisely against a surface, cut flush without a shoe, plunge into plasterboard to a controlled depth, and be stopped instantly. It is far slower and cannot cut heavy timber, but for undercutting door architraves, cutting out a socket opening or trimming a pipe against a wall it does in thirty seconds what a reciprocating saw does badly or not at all. Where a wall may contain services, the multi-tool's shallow controlled depth is materially safer.

For masonry, concrete and stone in any quantity, an angle grinder with a diamond blade, a cut-off saw or a wall chaser is the right tool, and for anything structural in concrete a diamond core drill or a specialist contractor. The reciprocating saw's carbide-grit blade is a get-out-of-trouble option for a handful of cuts, not a method. For felling and heavy timber, a chainsaw is faster by an order of magnitude, though a reciprocating saw with a pruning blade is genuinely safer for small limb work and for anyone untrained in chainsaw use.

Two situations call for stopping altogether rather than choosing another tool. The first is uncertainty about structure: a member whose load path is not understood should not be cut by anyone, and a temporary prop is cheaper than a collapse. The second is suspected asbestos, live services that cannot be verified as isolated, or an atmosphere that may contain gas. In all of these the correct action is to put the tool down and get the question answered by someone competent to answer it. The reciprocating saw's defining quality is that it removes material quickly and irreversibly in places you cannot see, and that quality is exactly why the judgement about when not to use it matters more than any technique for using it well. A cut that turns out to be wrong can be repaired in timber with a splice and in pipework with a coupling, but a severed cable buried in a wall, a nicked gas line or a compromised joist is a different order of problem, and the ten minutes spent establishing what lies behind the surface is reliably the cheapest ten minutes in the whole job.

guides.safetyNote: Power demolition is high-risk work. Always isolate the tool completely before changing blades, and verify that electrical circuits, gas and water services in the cutting area are isolated before cutting blind into any wall, floor or ceiling. Never cut a structural member without understanding what it supports and providing temporary support. Stop work immediately if you suspect asbestos-containing material, lead paint or a gas leak, and get a competent survey rather than proceeding carefully. Wear sealed eye protection, hearing protection, cut-resistant gloves and a properly fitted respirator matched to the dust, and manage hand-arm vibration exposure by limiting trigger time and keeping blades sharp. Blades and offcuts are extremely hot immediately after cutting.

guides.title: Oscillating Multi-Tools and Their Blades
guides.summary: How the oscillating multi-tool works, what its mounting systems and blade materials actually do, and how to choose, use and get the most life out of the accessories that make it useful.

sections.heading: What an Oscillating Multi-Tool Is For
sections.body:
An oscillating multi-tool is a power tool whose business end does not spin. Instead it rocks side to side through a very small angle, typically between one and four degrees in total, at somewhere between ten thousand and twenty thousand cycles a minute. A blade, scraper, rasp or sanding pad bolts to that oscillating head. The result is a machine that cuts, scrapes and sands, but which does none of those things faster than a tool purpose-built for the task. Its value lies entirely elsewhere.

The reason it exists is geometry. Every other cutting tool needs somewhere to put the part of itself that is not cutting. A circular saw needs a base plate and a blade guard and it cannot start a cut in the middle of a surface. A jigsaw needs clearance below the work for the blade to travel. A reciprocating saw needs a long run-up and throws its blade around violently. A handsaw needs room to swing. The oscillating multi-tool needs almost nothing: a blade projecting straight out from a slim head, moving through a few millimetres of arc, can start a cut in the centre of a sheet of plasterboard, cut flush against a floor with no clearance below, or reach into a fifteen-millimetre gap that no other powered tool can enter.

That capability turns a set of jobs that were previously slow, awkward hand work into fast machine work. Undercutting door casings so laminate flooring can slide beneath them. Cutting a socket opening in a wall that is already plastered. Trimming a protruding pipe flush with a wall. Removing hardened silicone from a bath edge, or grout from between tiles, without damaging the tiles. Cutting through nails buried inside a timber you cannot see into. Removing a damaged section from the middle of a floorboard without lifting the boards either side. In every one of these cases the alternative is either a chisel and a lot of patience or a tool that will damage the surrounding work.

The corresponding weaknesses are worth naming at the outset, because they explain most of the frustration people have with these machines. Cutting is slow, because the effective tooth speed is a fraction of that of a rotating blade. Heat, not sharpness, is usually what kills a blade. Consumables are expensive relative to the tool and are consumed quickly. Vibration transmitted into the hands is high enough to be a genuine occupational health issue over long sessions. And the accessory mounting systems have historically been a mess of incompatible patterns that costs buyers real money.

The practical conclusion, which experienced users reach quickly and beginners often resist, is that the multi-tool is a specialist rather than a general saw. It belongs in the kit as the tool you reach for when the shape of the problem, rather than the amount of material, is what makes the job hard. Bought on that understanding it repays its cost within a handful of jobs. Bought as a general-purpose cutting machine, it disappoints steadily and expensively.

sections.heading: The Mechanism: Turning Rotation Into a Small Arc
sections.body:
Inside the head is one of the simplest motion converters in power tools. The motor shaft carries an eccentric: a pin, or more usually a ball bearing, mounted off-centre so that as the shaft turns, the bearing traces a small circle. That bearing sits inside a fork or yoke, a two-pronged arm clamped to the output spindle. As the eccentric swings from one side of its circle to the other it pushes the fork left, then right. The spindle, and the blade bolted to it, therefore rocks back and forth once for every revolution of the motor. There is no clutch, no reciprocating rod and no gearbox in the conventional sense; the whole conversion happens in one moving joint, which is why the head can be made so slim.

Two numbers define the motion. The first is oscillation angle, the total angular sweep of the blade, quoted as something between about 1.4 and 4.2 degrees, with most general-purpose machines around 3.0 to 3.6. The second is oscillation frequency, in oscillations per minute, typically variable between roughly 5,000 and 20,000.

What matters at the workpiece is how far the teeth actually travel, and that depends on distance from the pivot. Arc length equals radius multiplied by angle in radians. A tooth 60 millimetres from the spindle centre on a machine with a 3.2 degree total sweep travels 60 multiplied by 0.0559 radians, which is about 3.4 millimetres from one extreme to the other. A full oscillation carries it out and back, so roughly 6.8 millimetres of travel per cycle. At 20,000 oscillations per minute, or 333 per second, that is about 2.3 metres per second of tooth speed.

Set that against a 190 millimetre circular saw blade at 5,000 revolutions per minute, whose teeth move at around 50 metres per second, and the character of the tool becomes clear. The multi-tool moves its teeth roughly twenty times more slowly, removes material at a correspondingly modest rate, and because the same few teeth pass through the same slot hundreds of times a second in a cut they cannot easily clear, the energy that does not become sawdust becomes heat concentrated in a very small volume of steel.

This also explains the design trade-off in oscillation angle. A wider sweep cuts faster and clears chips better, but it vibrates more, is harder to hold steady, and makes a plunge cut more likely to wander at the moment the blade first bites. Manufacturers aimed at fine work and detail sanding tend toward the lower end of the range; those aimed at demolition and heavy cutting toward the upper.

The same arithmetic explains why blade length matters. A tooth at the very tip of a long blade travels further per cycle than one close to the clamp, so a long blade cuts marginally faster at its extremity but is also under greater bending stress and dissipates more energy in flexing. This is why deep plunge blades are noticeably thicker than short ones, and why an over-long blade in a shallow cut feels vague and slow.

sections.heading: Where the Tool Came From
sections.body:
The oscillating principle reached the workshop by way of medicine. The German manufacturer C. and E. Fein, a firm with a long history in electrical engineering, developed an oscillating saw in the 1960s for cutting plaster casts off limbs. The problem it solved is instructive: a rotating blade would cut skin instantly, whereas a blade that moves only a couple of millimetres back and forth will happily saw through rigid plaster while soft, elastic tissue simply moves with it rather than being cut. Anyone who has had a cast removed has felt this counterintuitive property at work.

Fein launched the MultiMaster in the mid-1980s as a general-purpose tool for trades. For roughly two decades it had the market essentially to itself, protected by patents, sold at a professional price, and known chiefly to restorers, joiners and fitters who had met a job nothing else could do.

The key patents expired around 2008, and the market changed almost overnight. Bosch, which had already been working with Fein, brought out its GOP range. Dremel launched the Multi-Max, aimed squarely at the domestic user. Rockwell marketed the SoniCrafter, Makita, Milwaukee, DeWalt, Metabo, Festool and eventually every own-brand budget line followed. Within a few years the multi-tool went from a specialist import to something sold in supermarkets, and prices fell by an order of magnitude at the low end.

The consequence that still shapes the market is accessory compatibility. Fein's original mounting pattern, later called the Oscillating Interface System, used a twelve-point star recess that located on matching pins in the tool head. As competitors arrived, many invented their own patterns, partly for genuine engineering reasons and largely to sell their own consumables. Buyers ended up with drawers of blades that fitted one machine and not another.

Two things eased it. Third-party manufacturers began producing open-ended, slotted universal hubs designed to drop over most pin patterns, and adapter plates appeared for the rest. Then in 2016 Fein and Bosch jointly introduced Starlock, a three-dimensional conical interface intended to replace the flat star. The claim behind Starlock is that a form-fit conical seat transmits torque through a much larger contact area than a flat plate clamped by a single bolt, allowing more power to be delivered without the accessory slipping or the hub wearing round. It comes in three escalating sizes, Starlock, StarlockPlus and StarlockMax, with larger machines accepting smaller accessories but not the reverse.

What the whole history leaves behind is a market with two distinct halves. At the top, professional machines from Fein, Bosch, Festool, Makita and Milwaukee are genuinely well engineered, with serviceable bearings, effective vibration damping and electronics that hold speed under load. At the bottom, an enormous number of visually similar machines are assembled from the same few generic designs and rebadged, and among these the differences are largely cosmetic. The blades, however, come from a far smaller number of factories than the tools do, which is why third-party consumables are often indistinguishable from branded ones.

sections.heading: Anatomy of the Machine
sections.body:
Strip the housing off a multi-tool and there is remarkably little inside, which is why the category spans such an enormous price range for outwardly similar objects.

At the back sits the motor. On mains-powered machines this is a universal brushed motor rated somewhere between 180 and 450 watts. On cordless machines it is either a brushed motor or, increasingly, a brushless one. In front of it is the eccentric and fork assembly, running in two bearings, and ahead of that the output spindle carrying the accessory clamp. Around the head is a vibration-damped grip area, because the whole front of the tool is shaking several thousand times a second and the housing has to isolate the user's hand from as much of that as possible.

Quality differences concentrate in three places. The first is bearing specification and the rigidity of the fork. Cheap tools use undersized bearings and a stamped fork that flexes, so a proportion of the intended oscillation is absorbed inside the machine rather than delivered to the blade; the tool feels blunt even with a new accessory, and the bearings become noisy within a few dozen hours. The second is thermal management. A multi-tool spends its life stalled or near-stalled against material, which is the worst case for a universal motor, and machines without adequate airflow past the field windings cook themselves. The third is the accessory clamp. A worn or poorly hardened hub allows the blade to creep, which rounds off the drive pattern on both the blade and the tool and eventually makes both useless.

Clamping arrangements have improved markedly. Early tools used a hex bolt and a loose washer, easy to drop into a joist void. Most machines now use a tool-free lever, which matters more than it sounds because a busy job may involve twenty accessory changes and a hot blade cannot be handled comfortably.

Two ergonomic details separate good tools from irritating ones. One is whether the accessory can be mounted at intervals around the spindle, usually every thirty degrees, so that a blade can be angled to reach into a corner or set perpendicular for a flush cut. The other is the position and feel of the variable speed control, which needs to be adjustable without letting go of the tool. A worklight on the head is genuinely useful, since most multi-tool work happens in exactly the dark cramped places where you cannot see the cut line.

A few machines add genuinely functional extras. Depth stops, offered as accessory shoes on some professional models, let a plunge cut be made to a set depth repeatedly, which matters when cutting a slot in a floor above a service void. Dust extraction shrouds clamp around the head and route debris to a vacuum port, and although they add bulk they are close to essential for any mineral cutting. Guide rails and plunge attachments exist for cutting straight lines in sheet material, though at that point a track saw is usually the better answer.

sections.heading: Corded, Cordless and Brushless
sections.body:
The choice between mains and battery power matters more for this tool than for most, because of how it is used.

Corded machines have one significant advantage beyond price: they will run at full power indefinitely without a battery to flatten or a thermal cutout to trip. For work such as removing a large area of tile adhesive or grout, where the tool runs continuously for tens of minutes under near-stall load, this is a real benefit. They are also lighter in the hand, since a battery pack of any usefulness adds 400 to 800 grams at the back of the tool, which changes the balance of a machine that is often held one-handed above head height or at arm's length.

Cordless machines win on almost everything else. Multi-tool work is characteristically short bursts in awkward places: under a sink, in a loft, at the foot of a door frame, on a roof. A trailing lead in those places is not merely annoying but is a genuine hazard, and the tool is frequently used exactly where the cut will remove something the cable is lying on. Modern 18 volt platforms deliver enough power that the difference is not felt on ordinary cutting, though sustained heavy grinding will still flatten a 2 amp-hour pack quickly. A 4 or 5 amp-hour pack is a reasonable minimum for anything beyond occasional use.

Brushless motors matter here more than marketing usually manages to explain. A brushed motor makes electrical contact through carbon blocks pressed against a rotating commutator, which wear, arc and waste energy as friction and heat. A brushless motor commutates electronically, so it has no wearing contacts, converts a higher proportion of battery energy into work, and, critically for this application, can be controlled precisely by its driver. The practical benefits in a multi-tool are longer runtime per charge, a motor that survives the near-stall duty cycle far better, constant-speed electronics that hold the set oscillation rate as load increases, and electronic overload protection that shuts the tool down before something melts. The downside is cost and the fact that a failed controller is usually not economically repairable, whereas brushes are a five-minute replacement.

There is one further consideration for anyone buying a first cordless tool: the battery platform is a much bigger commitment than the tool. Batteries cost a large fraction of a tool's price, are not interchangeable between manufacturers, and are the component that ages out first, typically after three to five years or several hundred charge cycles. A multi-tool is a poor reason to enter an ecosystem on its own, and a good reason to stay in one you already own.

For the occasional domestic user with an existing cordless drill from a mainstream brand, a bare-tool multi-tool on that platform is almost always the best value available. For someone with no cordless tools at all who needs the machine for one project, a corded model at a third of the price is the rational purchase.

sections.heading: Mounting Systems and the Compatibility Problem
sections.body:
Before buying any accessory, you need to know which interface your machine uses, because a blade that does not seat properly will either refuse to fit or, worse, fit loosely and destroy both itself and the tool hub within minutes.

The original and still most widespread flat pattern is Fein's Oscillating Interface System, universally shortened to OIS. It presents a circular recess with twelve radial teeth arranged like a star, which engage matching pins or a raised star on the tool spindle, with a bolt through the centre clamping the accessory down. Bosch adopted the same footprint, so OIS became a de facto standard across a large part of the market.

A second family, common on Makita, Milwaukee, DeWalt, Metabo and many others, uses its own pin arrangements. Some are close variants of OIS; others are entirely different. The market's practical answer has been the universal or quick-fit hub: an accessory whose mounting area is cut as an open-ended slotted pattern, a sort of keyhole with radiating slots, that will drop over most common pin layouts and be clamped down without needing the bolt fully removed. The majority of third-party blades sold today use this hub, and it is the safe default for a mixed workshop.

Starlock, introduced jointly by Fein and Bosch in 2016, is a genuine engineering change rather than a proprietary annoyance. Instead of a flat plate clamped by a bolt, the accessory has a conical, three-dimensionally formed seat that drops into a matching cone on the tool and is held by a lever-operated clamp. Because torque is transmitted across a formed three-dimensional surface rather than by friction between two flat faces, the manufacturers claim substantially higher torque transmission without slip. The system is tiered: Starlock is the smallest, then StarlockPlus, then StarlockMax for the largest and most powerful machines. A machine of a given tier accepts accessories of that tier and every smaller one, but not larger. Starlock-footprint accessories will also physically mount on many older OIS machines, which softens the transition.

Adapters exist to fit OIS accessories to non-OIS machines and vice versa, and they work, but with a caveat worth taking seriously. Every adapter adds a joint, and a joint adds compliance, backlash and thickness. Compliance absorbs oscillation; backlash hammers the mating faces; and the extra few millimetres of stack changes the geometry of a flush cut. An adapter is a reasonable way to use up a stock of legacy blades and a poor way to run a tool permanently.

One practical check is worth doing before any bulk accessory order. Remove a blade from the machine, photograph the drive face of the tool spindle and the mounting recess of the blade, and compare them against the diagrams that reputable accessory sellers publish. The mounting patterns are distinctive enough to identify by eye, and getting this wrong on a multipack of twenty blades is an expensive mistake that is rarely worth the postage to correct.

sections.heading: Blade Metallurgy: What the Letters Mean
sections.body:
Blade packaging is covered in abbreviations, and they are the single most useful thing to understand, because choosing the wrong material wastes both the blade and the job.

HCS stands for high carbon steel. The blade is made from a single hardened steel of roughly 0.8 to 1.0 per cent carbon, heat treated to something around 60 on the Rockwell C scale. It is cheap, it can be given very sharp aggressive teeth, and in clean softwood, plywood, plasterboard and plastics it cuts faster than anything else in the range. Its weakness is absolute: contact with a single nail, screw or staple will strip or blunt the teeth immediately, because hardened carbon steel is not appreciably harder than a hardened fastener and loses its temper if it gets hot.

BiM means bi-metal, and it is the workhorse of the category. The tooth strip is high speed steel, most often the cobalt-bearing grade designated M42, which retains its hardness at temperatures that would soften carbon steel. That strip is electron-beam welded to a back made from a tough spring steel such as a chrome-vanadium grade. The result exploits both properties: the hard tooth edge resists wear and heat, while the flexible back absorbs the bending and shock that would snap a fully hardened blade. A bi-metal blade will cut nails, screws, thin sheet metal, copper pipe and nail-embedded reclaimed timber, and will survive being levered slightly in a cut.

Carbide-tipped blades carry brazed tungsten carbide teeth on a steel body. Tungsten carbide is far harder than any steel and holds an edge at temperatures that would ruin high speed steel, so these blades handle hardened screws, cast iron, fibre cement board, stainless steel and heavily abrasive materials. They typically cost three to five times a bi-metal blade and last far longer in those materials, but carbide is brittle: a tooth that is levered or twisted chips off rather than bending.

Carbide-grit and diamond-grit accessories have no teeth at all; the working edge carries bonded tungsten carbide particles or electroplated diamond. They abrade rather than cut, and are correct for tile grout, backer board, glass-reinforced plastic, brick, stone and porcelain. Diamond cuts harder material and lasts longer; carbide grit is cheaper and adequate for ordinary cement grout.

The general economy is that HCS costs very little and dies instantly on metal, bi-metal costs a few times more and handles almost everything in construction timber, and carbide or diamond costs several times more again and is the only thing that works on mineral and hardened material. As a rough guide to expectations, a carbon steel blade might cut twenty or thirty metres of clean softwood before it stops being useful, and nothing at all after meeting one nail; a good bi-metal blade will cut through dozens of embedded fasteners; a carbide plunge blade will go through hardened screws that stop bi-metal dead.

One further label appears on packaging: HSS, plain high speed steel throughout. These blades are hard but brittle, and are mostly encountered in fine metal-cutting sizes.

sections.heading: Teeth: Pitch, Set, Kerf and Geometry
sections.body:
Beyond the material, the shape and spacing of the teeth determine how a blade behaves, and the differences are large enough that two bi-metal blades of the same size can feel like different tools.

Tooth pitch is usually expressed as teeth per inch. A coarse blade of eight to twelve teeth per inch has large gullets, the spaces between teeth, which carry sawdust out of the cut. Coarse pitch cuts wood fast and clears chips well but leaves a rough edge and grabs in thin material. A fine blade of eighteen to twenty-four teeth per inch produces a smoother cut with small chips, which is what thin metal, plastic and delicate trim require.

The governing rule, inherited from all sawing, is that at least three teeth should be engaged in the material at any moment. Fewer than that and the workpiece drops into a gullet, the next tooth strikes it as an impact rather than a cut, and teeth strip off. This is why cutting a one-millimetre steel sheet with a ten teeth per inch blade destroys the blade almost immediately, and why cutting a fifty-millimetre timber with a twenty-four teeth per inch blade merely produces heat and no progress, since the tiny gullets pack solid with dust within a few strokes and the blade then rubs rather than cuts.

Set is the sideways splaying of alternate teeth so that the slot they cut, the kerf, is wider than the body of the blade behind them. Without set, the blade body binds against the cut walls, friction rises sharply, heat builds and the blade may seize or snap. A typical multi-tool blade body is around 0.9 to 1.1 millimetres thick and cuts a kerf of 1.2 to 1.4 millimetres. Some fine metal-cutting blades use a wavy set, where the tooth strip is gently corrugated rather than individual teeth bent, which distributes load across more teeth in thin material.

Tooth geometry proper varies more than most users notice. Standard alternating bevel teeth suit general work. So-called Japanese-tooth blades, offered by several manufacturers, use long raked teeth with deep gullets on hardened carbon steel and cut wood remarkably fast, at the cost of being useless the moment they touch a fastener. Metal-cutting blades use a much smaller rake angle, sometimes near zero or slightly negative, because a positive rake tooth digs into steel, grabs and chips. Blades sold for plunge cutting often have teeth extending around the tip corners so the blade can enter the work end-on rather than only along its edge.

A final geometric detail that is rarely discussed but strongly affects feel is blade thickness. Thin blades, around 0.8 millimetres, cut a narrow kerf, remove less material and therefore cut faster for a given power, but they flex under side load and wander in deep cuts. Thick blades of 1.4 millimetres and up track straight and survive rough handling but demand noticeably more power. Blades intended for accurate flush work tend to be thin; blades sold for demolition are thick.

sections.heading: Blade Shapes and What Each One Is For
sections.body:
Multi-tool accessories come in a small number of recognisable outlines, and each shape exists because of a specific geometric problem.

The plunge or straight blade is the standard rectangular item, commonly 32 or 35 millimetres wide with a straight toothed end, also offered at 20 millimetres for tight work and 65 for faster progress in sheet material. Because the teeth are on the end, it drives straight into the face of a board, which is the capability the tool is bought for. Typical depth of cut is 40 to 45 millimetres.

The segment blade is a semicircular arc, usually about 85 to 88 millimetres across, toothed along the curved edge. Because the cutting edge lies on an arc centred on the spindle, the whole edge moves tangentially through the cut, which gives a much longer effective cutting edge than a straight blade and cuts long straight lines faster. It is also the standard carrier for grout-removal and tile work in carbide or diamond grit. It cannot plunge into the middle of a surface, but it excels at extending an existing cut and at flush-cutting along a face.

Round or circular blades, a full disc mounted so only part of the circumference works, suit long straight cuts in sheet material and cutting close to a corner. Rotating a worn disc to a fresh sector extends its life several times, which is their main attraction.

Scrapers come in two stiffnesses. A rigid scraper is a thick, chisel-like blade for removing hardened adhesive, paint, mortar residue and old vinyl or carpet backing; it behaves like a power chisel and will gouge softwood if allowed. A flexible scraper is thin and springy, for lifting silicone, soft caulk and wallpaper without cutting the surface underneath.

Rasps and carbide-coated files, usually triangular or finger-shaped, remove wood, plaster and filler by abrasion rather than cutting, and suit enlarging an opening slightly or working back a rough edge where a sanding pad cannot reach.

The sanding pad, a triangular hook-and-loop platen roughly 93 millimetres on a side, converts the machine into a detail sander. The oscillating action makes it noticeably more aggressive than an orbital sander of similar size, and rather more prone to leaving marks, but it reaches into corners nothing else will enter. Sheets are held by hook-and-loop backing and can be rotated so that a worn tip is swapped for a fresh edge, which triples the useful life of each one.

Two further shapes are worth knowing. Long-reach or extended blades put the teeth 90 millimetres or more from the clamp, allowing a cut through a thick assembly or deep into a recess where the tool body will not fit. And offset or cranked blades set the cutting edge in a plane below the mounting face, so the blade can lie genuinely flat on a floor without the clamp nut lifting it, which is what makes a truly flush cut possible. Anyone undercutting door casings should own one, because a straight blade held flat sits a few millimetres proud.

sections.heading: Technique: How to Cut Without Destroying the Blade
sections.body:
More blades are killed by technique than by wear, and the errors are consistent enough to be worth learning deliberately.

The dominant one is pressure. The instinct when a cut is slow is to push harder. On a multi-tool this is counterproductive in a way that is easy to explain mechanically. The head oscillates through a fixed angle only as long as the motor can drive it against the resistance of the cut. Push beyond that and the amplitude collapses; the blade stops travelling far enough to clear chips from its gullets, so it rubs instead of cutting, and essentially all the input energy becomes heat in a strip of steel a few millimetres wide. Blade temperature climbs past the tempering point of the tooth material within seconds, the teeth soften, and the blade is finished. The visible evidence is a blue or straw discolouration along the tooth line, which is permanent and means the hardness is gone. The correct pressure is light, roughly the weight of the tool plus a little, with the operator's job being to hold the line rather than to force progress.

The second technique that transforms blade life is lateral movement. Rather than holding the blade in one spot, sweep it gently side to side along the length of the cut, or rock it slightly. This spreads the work across the whole tooth line instead of wearing a notch in one place, keeps fresh teeth entering material, and gives chips somewhere to go. It also lets air reach the steel between passes. A blade used in one fixed spot will wear a smooth concave hollow that then rubs and cannot cut at all, while the rest of the edge is still sharp.

Starting a plunge cut needs its own method. Rather than presenting the blade flat and pushing it in, tilt the tool so only the leading corner of the blade contacts the surface, let that corner cut a shallow groove, and then rotate the tool down until the blade is perpendicular and fully in the kerf. Presenting it flat causes the blade to skate across the surface and score the finish before it bites.

Speed should be matched to material. Wood and plasterboard take maximum speed. Plastics and laminates need reduced speed, because heat melts the material, which then welds into the gullets and stops the blade dead. Metal is cut at low to medium speed, since high oscillation rates generate temperatures that ruin the teeth. Some users add a drop of cutting oil for steel, which helps, though on a plunge cut in a wall it is often impractical.

Finally, clear the cut. Withdraw the blade periodically to shed dust, especially in plaster and in deep timber, where packed dust is a major source of heat.

sections.heading: The Jobs Nothing Else Can Do
sections.body:
It is worth being concrete about where the multi-tool is genuinely irreplaceable, because that list is short and everything outside it is usually better done another way.

Undercutting door casings and architraves is the classic. When a hard floor is fitted, it must run beneath the door frame rather than being scribed around it, both because a butt joint against a casing looks poor and because a floating floor must be free to move. A segment or flush-cut blade laid flat on an offcut of the flooring, used as a height gauge, cuts the casing horizontally at exactly the right height in a few seconds. The alternative, a hand jamb saw, works but is slow and hard to keep level.

Cutting openings in installed surfaces is the second. A socket or switch box opening in plasterboard that is already fixed and skimmed, an access hatch in a ceiling, a hole in a fitted panel for a pipe: all of these need a cut that starts in the middle of a surface with no room behind it. A plunge blade does it without a pilot hole, and unlike a jigsaw does not need the shoe to be flat on the surface.

Flush cutting is the third. Protruding fixings, dowels, bolts, pipe stubs and stubborn screws can be cut off level with a surface without the tool body fouling anything, because the blade can be mounted perpendicular to the tool axis. A bi-metal or carbide blade will take off a rusted bolt in a place a grinder cannot reach and would burn everything nearby.

Nail-embedded and reclaimed timber is the fourth. Any other saw is ruined by hidden fasteners; a bi-metal multi-tool blade simply cuts them, which makes it the standard tool for demolition trimming, for cutting out a rotten section of stud between fixings, and for working reclaimed boards.

Removing set material is the fifth: silicone from a bath edge, grout from between tiles you want to keep, old adhesive from a floor screed, paint runs from a moulding, mortar from a joint to be repointed. A rigid scraper or a diamond-grit blade removes these with far more control than a chisel and far less collateral damage than a grinder.

Outside these, the tool is usually the wrong choice. It will cut a sheet of plywood, but a circular saw does it in a tenth of the time with a straighter edge. It will sand, but any dedicated sander is better on open surfaces. It will cut a pipe, but a pipe cutter gives a square end. Treating it as a general saw is the commonest way to spend a great deal of money on consumables for no reason.

A useful test before reaching for it: ask whether the difficulty is the quantity of material or the access to it. Quantity is a job for a bigger tool; access is a job for this one.

sections.heading: Building a Blade Kit Worth Owning
sections.body:
Most multi-tools are sold with a token accessory set that is almost entirely high carbon steel and a sanding pad, and most of it is used once. A deliberately chosen small kit will outperform a large assorted box, because the assorted boxes are padded with duplicates of the cheapest items.

The buying principle is that blade quality matters far more than tool quality on this machine. A budget tool with good blades will out-cut an expensive tool with cheap ones, because the accessory is where the work actually happens and where nearly all the failure occurs. Reputable third-party manufacturers produce bi-metal and carbide blades at well below the tool makers' own prices, and for anything other than the most demanding professional use they are a sensible economy. The place not to economise is anything carrying carbide or diamond, where cheap products often use thin coatings that strip within a few minutes of use.

Sizes to note when ordering: standard plunge blades are usually 32 or 35 millimetres wide; a 20 millimetre blade reaches into narrow slots; a 65 millimetre wide blade covers ground faster in sheet material. Segment blades are typically 85 to 88 millimetres across. Sanding sheets for the triangular pad are around 93 millimetres per side. Check whether your machine takes OIS, a proprietary pattern, a universal slotted hub or Starlock before ordering anything.
ingredients: Bi-metal plunge blades, 32 or 35 millimetres wide, in a multipack. This is the item you will use most. Buy them five or ten at a time; they are consumable and the per-blade price falls sharply with quantity.
One or two wide bi-metal plunge blades at 65 millimetres, for faster progress in plasterboard, plywood and stud walls where the cut is not confined.
A narrow 10 to 20 millimetre bi-metal blade for slots, tight corners and cutting close to an obstruction.
High carbon steel wood blades, coarse-toothed or Japanese-tooth, bought cheaply in bulk. They cut clean timber noticeably faster than bi-metal and are treated as disposable.
A bi-metal segment blade, roughly 85 millimetres, for flush cuts along a surface and for extending existing cuts in a straight line.
A carbide-tipped plunge blade for hardened screws, nail plates, cast iron, stainless fixings and fibre cement board.
A diamond-grit or carbide-grit segment blade for tile grout, cement backer board, stone and mortar joints.
A rigid scraper for hardened adhesive, paint and mortar residue, plus a flexible scraper for silicone and soft sealant.
The triangular sanding pad with an assortment of hook-and-loop sheets in 60, 80, 120 and 180 grit.
A spare clamping bolt and washer if your tool uses them, since these are easily dropped and lost on site, and a hex key kept taped to the tool or its case.

sections.heading: A Worked Procedure: Undercutting a Door Casing
sections.body:
This is the job most people buy the tool for, and doing it accurately takes about two minutes per casing. The aim is a horizontal cut through the door casing and any architrave, at exactly the height of the finished floor plus its underlay, so the flooring can slide underneath and leave no visible gap.

The critical number is the gauge height. It must equal the total thickness of everything that will sit under the flooring surface at that point: the underlay plus the board thickness, and nothing else. Cut too high and there is a visible slot above the floor. Cut too low and the board will not go under, which is far harder to fix. Work out the stack before you start and check it against the actual materials rather than the packaging.

Before cutting, establish what is behind the casing. Door frames often sit against masonry, and there may be fixings, packers or a metal frame. A bi-metal blade is the safe default because it survives hitting a nail; a high carbon steel blade will be destroyed by the first fixing.
steps: Remove any existing skirting or floor covering in the doorway so the subfloor is exposed and level, and vacuum the area so the gauge piece sits flat rather than on grit.

Cut a short offcut of the actual flooring, about 200 millimetres long, and lay it face down on the subfloor next to the casing, with a piece of the actual underlay beneath it if underlay will be used. This stack is your height gauge.
Fit a bi-metal segment or flush-cut blade and mount it so it sits flat against the gauge, perpendicular to the tool body, with the tool held horizontally.

Rest the blade flat on the gauge offcut, with the teeth touching the face of the casing. Check by eye along the length of the blade that it is lying flat and not tipped, because a tilted blade cuts a sloping line that shows.

Start the tool at full speed before the teeth touch, then advance gently, letting the blade's own weight and the gauge beneath it hold the height. Do not press down; downward pressure bows the blade and cuts below the line.

Work across the full width of the casing and any architrave, sweeping the blade slightly along its length to spread the wear. Stop when the blade is through the timber and just contacting whatever is behind it.
Slide the gauge along and repeat for the opposite side of the doorway, then for any architrave returns, keeping the same offcut so every cut is at an identical height.
Knock out the waste piece with a chisel or screwdriver, and pare back any fibres in the corners with a sharp chisel so the flooring slides in without catching.
Test-fit an offcut of flooring under the cut before laying the floor. If it fouls, remove a further millimetre with the blade rather than forcing the board, which will crack the tongue.

sections.heading: Dust, Vibration and Protecting Yourself
sections.body:
The multi-tool creates two occupational hazards that are easy to underestimate because the machine is small and quiet compared with a grinder or a breaker.

The first is dust. Cutting or grinding tile, grout, mortar, concrete backer board, brick, stone or engineered stone releases respirable crystalline silica, particles small enough to reach the deepest part of the lung, where they cause irreversible scarring known as silicosis and substantially raise lung cancer risk. The workplace exposure limit in Great Britain is 0.1 milligrams per cubic metre averaged over eight hours, and in the United States the permissible limit is 0.05, figures that dry cutting indoors will exceed within minutes. Control means extraction at the tool, water suppression where practical, and, where dust cannot be eliminated, respiratory protection of at least FFP3 or an equivalent half-mask with P3 filters, correctly fitted against bare skin. A cloth or surgical mask does nothing at all against particles of this size.

Older buildings carry two further specific hazards. Asbestos was used in floor tiles and their bitumen adhesive, in textured ceiling coatings, in insulating board, in pipe lagging and in cement sheet, and cutting or abrading any of these with a power tool creates an extremely hazardous release. Nothing in a pre-2000 building should be cut with this tool until you know what it is. Paint applied before the late 1970s may contain lead, which sanding or scraping will disperse.

The second hazard is vibration. Multi-tools typically report vibration magnitudes in the range of about 8 to 15 metres per second squared at the handle, and the tool is held tightly in one or both hands by design. Under the UK Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005, the daily exposure action value is 2.5 metres per second squared normalised over eight hours and the exposure limit value is 5. Because the calculation goes with the square of magnitude, the arithmetic is brutal: at a declared 10 metres per second squared, the limit value is reached after only 5 squared divided by 10 squared, multiplied by eight hours, which is two hours of actual trigger time. Prolonged overexposure causes hand-arm vibration syndrome, with permanent numbness, loss of grip strength and painful blanching of the fingers in cold weather. Practical control means keeping trigger time short, gripping no harder than necessary, keeping blades sharp so cuts finish faster, keeping hands warm, and rotating tasks.

Noise is a lesser but real issue, typically in the high eighties to mid nineties of A-weighted decibels, which warrants hearing protection for any sustained session. Eye protection is non-negotiable: blade teeth and carbide tips do break off and leave at speed, and the tool is frequently used at or above head height where debris falls directly into the eyes. Gloves are a more nuanced question: they reduce the transmission of some vibration frequencies and protect against a hot blade, but they also reduce the tactile feedback that tells you a cut is binding.

sections.heading: Getting More Life Out of Consumables
sections.body:
Blades are the running cost of this tool, and a few habits change how long they last by a factor of several.

Match the blade to the material honestly. The commonest waste is a bi-metal blade in clean timber, where a cheap carbon steel blade cuts faster for a fraction of the price, and the reverse error of a carbon steel blade where fasteners might lurk. If there is any chance of metal, start with bi-metal.

Keep the cut cool. Heat is what destroys tooth hardness, and the tempering point of high speed steel teeth is well above that of carbon steel but is still reachable within seconds of a stalled cut. Work in bursts, withdraw the blade to let air over it, and if a blade is too hot to touch, stop and let it cool rather than continuing. Cutting metal at reduced oscillation speed rather than maximum makes a very large difference.

Use the whole edge. Because most people cut in a single spot, blades routinely reach the bin with two thirds of their teeth unused and a hollow worn in the middle. Deliberately move the contact point along the blade. On round blades, slacken the clamp and rotate the disc a few degrees when the working sector dulls; the same disc can be indexed round several times.

Do not lever. The blade is designed to be loaded along its length and shaken sideways, not twisted. Levering to widen a kerf cracks bi-metal blades at the weld and shears carbide teeth off their braze. If a cut binds, withdraw and re-enter rather than prying.

Keep the clamp tight and the hub clean. A blade that creeps under load rounds off its own drive pattern and the tool's, and once the drive faces are worn the blade will never seat properly again. Brush dust out of the recess before fitting, and check the clamp after the first minute of a heavy cut, since blades bed in and can loosen.

Resharpening is generally not economic, since bi-metal teeth are too small and too hard to file usefully and the set cannot be restored by hand. Carbide-grit and diamond-grit accessories can often be revived, however: rubbing the loaded face on a dressing stone or coarse concrete clears packed grout and exposes fresh grit, which can double the life of an expensive segment.

Finally, store blades so they do not knock together. Loose blades in a toolbox chip each other's teeth, and a chipped tooth becomes a stress raiser where a crack starts. A cheap plastic wallet or a strip of foam with slots cut in it solves this, and keeping blades sorted by material also stops the classic mistake of grabbing a carbon steel blade for a cut that will meet a nail.

It is also worth keeping partially worn blades rather than binning them. A blade too dull for accurate work is often perfectly serviceable for rough demolition where the cut face will never be seen, and using a spent blade for the dirty part of a job preserves a sharp one for the part that matters.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and Troubleshooting
sections.body:
When a multi-tool underperforms, the cause is nearly always one of a short list, and the symptoms distinguish them clearly.

If the tool runs at full speed but barely cuts, and the blade is not obviously blunt, suspect the drive interface. A worn hub or an under-tightened clamp lets the blade slip fractionally on every oscillation, so most of the motion never reaches the teeth. Look at the blade's mounting recess: if the star points or slot edges are rounded and shiny, the blade has been creeping. Look at the tool's drive face for the same rounding. Adapter plates are frequent culprits.

If the tool bogs down under light pressure and the head gets very hot, the likely causes are a packed or glazed blade, or excessive pressure collapsing the oscillation amplitude. Withdraw, inspect the gullets, and clear them; a blade full of melted plastic or set adhesive cannot cut at all.

If the blade cracks, look at where. A crack starting at the root of the mounting slot usually means the clamp was loose and the blade was hammering. A crack along the bi-metal weld line means it was levered or twisted. Teeth stripped clean off in a row usually means too few teeth engaged in thin material, or a carbon steel blade meeting a fastener.

If the tool loses power intermittently and smells hot, a brushed motor may have worn brushes, which are cheap and often user-replaceable, or the armature may be failing. On a brushless machine, intermittent shutdown is more often the electronic overload protection doing its job, which means the duty cycle is too aggressive rather than that the tool is faulty. Let it idle for a minute with no load, since running fans is how these tools cool.

If the head becomes rattly or noisy with a whine that changes with speed, the eccentric bearing is failing. On better tools this is a serviceable part; on inexpensive ones it usually is not, and the machine is at the end of its life.

If cuts wander or come out sloping, the fault is normally technique rather than hardware: a blade presented flat rather than tipped in at the start, downward pressure bowing a long blade, or a gauge piece resting on debris.

Two situations call for stopping rather than troubleshooting. If you are cutting into a wall, floor or ceiling and do not know with certainty what is behind it, stop and find out, because live cables, gas pipes and water pipes are all routinely buried at exactly the depths this tool reaches. And if the material is unidentified and the building predates the year 2000, treat it as potentially asbestos-containing until proved otherwise. In both cases the cost of checking is minutes; the cost of not checking can be a flooded room, an electric shock or an exposure that shows up thirty years later.

guides.safetyNote: Before plunging into any wall, floor or ceiling, establish what lies behind it: cables, gas and water pipes sit within the depth this tool cuts, and a detector plus isolation of the circuit is the minimum precaution. Do not cut or abrade unidentified materials in buildings predating 2000, since asbestos was used in floor tiles and their adhesive, textured coatings, insulating board, pipe lagging and cement sheet; disturbing it with a power tool is extremely hazardous. Cutting tile, grout, mortar, stone or cement board releases respirable crystalline silica and requires extraction, water suppression or at least FFP3 respiratory protection, not a cloth mask. Wear eye protection at all times, because teeth and carbide tips do break off; use hearing protection for sustained work; and limit trigger time, since typical vibration levels of 8 to 15 metres per second squared can reach the legal daily exposure limit in roughly two hours and cause permanent nerve and circulatory damage. Blades reach temperatures that will burn skin instantly; let them cool or use pliers to change them.

guides.title: Router Basics for Home Woodwork
guides.summary: How to use a woodworking router safely and well: fixed-base versus plunge, choosing and setting bits, cut depth, feed direction, edge profiling, grooves and dados, template routing, the router table, and safe habits.

sections.heading: What a Router Is and What It Does
sections.body:
A router is a woodworking power tool that spins a cutting bit at very high speed — typically between sixteen thousand and twenty-four thousand revolutions per minute — to shape, trim, hollow, and profile wood. The name comes from the old sense of "to rout out," meaning to gouge or scoop material away, and that is exactly what the tool does: a bit projecting below a flat base cuts a channel or an edge as you guide the machine along the workpiece. Unlike a saw, which parts wood along a single line, a router removes material in a controlled path of almost any shape, which is why it is one of the most versatile tools in a workshop.

The tool has two broad families. A fixed-base router holds the bit at a set depth that you dial in before you begin; the base does not move during the cut, so the depth stays constant. A plunge router rides on two spring-loaded posts that let you push the spinning bit down into the middle of a board and then retract it, which is essential for stopped grooves, mortises, and inlays that do not run off the edge. Many kits sell a single motor with both bases so you can swap between them.

At the heart of the machine is the collet, a split metal sleeve that grips the shank of the bit when a nut is tightened around it. Collets come in two common sizes, quarter inch and half inch, and the larger size grips more firmly and resists the deflection that spoils a cut. Above the collet sits the motor, and around it a housing you hold or that clamps into a table. Understanding these parts — collet, base, depth mechanism, and motor — is the foundation for every technique that follows, because nearly every mistake beginners make traces back to a loose collet, a wrong depth, or a base that was not held flat.

Routers come in a range of sizes that suit different work. A full-size router of two to three and a quarter horsepower has the mass and torque for large bits and heavy joinery, and lives happily in a table. A compact or trim router, often sold as a palm router, runs a quarter-inch collet, weighs a fraction as much, and is controlled with one hand, which makes it ideal for small edge profiles, laminate trimming, and delicate freehand work where a heavy machine would be clumsy. At the industrial end, the same cutting principle drives a CNC router, where a computer moves the spinning bit through a programmed path; understanding the handheld tool is the foundation for that automated work too. Knowing which size of router suits a job — heavy machine for hogging, trim router for finesse — is part of using the tool well rather than fighting it.

sections.heading: Fixed-Base and Plunge Routers Compared
sections.body:
Choosing between a fixed-base and a plunge router, or deciding which to reach for on a given job, comes down to where the cut starts and ends. A fixed-base router excels at edge work: rounding over a tabletop, cutting a decorative moulding along a shelf, or trimming a laminate flush to a substrate. Because the depth is locked, the tool is predictable and easy to balance on a narrow edge, and it is generally lighter and lower in profile than a plunge model, which makes it more comfortable for long runs of edge profiling. Mounted upside down in a router table, a fixed base is the standard configuration, since the table itself sets the height and you no longer need to plunge.

A plunge router earns its keep whenever a cut must begin in the interior of a board rather than at an edge. To make a stopped dado — a groove that starts and finishes partway across a shelf — you position the tool over the start point, switch on the motor, and press the body down so the bit descends into the wood to a preset stop, then travel to the end and retract. Mortises for door hinges and joinery, signs routed into a plaque, and inlay recesses all depend on this plunging action. The trade-off is weight and a higher centre of gravity, which can feel tippy on a thin edge.

Many woodworkers own a combination kit precisely so they are not forced to choose. The motor lifts out of one base and drops into the other in under a minute. If you are buying your first router and can own only one, a mid-size plunge router of around two horsepower is the more flexible choice, because it can do edge work adequately while also handling interior cuts a fixed base cannot, whereas a fixed base simply cannot plunge. Serious edge-profiling volume, though, is where a dedicated fixed base or a compact trim router shines.

A third member of the family deserves mention: the compact trim router, which is usually a fixed-base design in miniature and has become many woodworkers' most-reached-for tool. Its light weight and low centre of gravity give exceptional control for edge rounding and flush trimming, and plunge bases are available for it when interior cuts are needed. Whichever base you use, the balance of the tool in the cut is what determines control, and that balance shifts as the router passes off the end of a board or over a narrow edge where less of the base is supported. Experienced users learn to keep firm downward and inward pressure so the base never rocks, to support the router with an offcut of the same thickness clamped alongside a narrow workpiece, and to plan the path so the base is always resting on solid material rather than teetering on an edge.

sections.heading: Router Bits: Types and Anatomy
sections.body:
A router does nothing without a bit, and the range of bits is what makes the tool so versatile. Every bit shares the same basic anatomy: a shank that the collet grips, a body, and one or more cutting edges, usually of carbide brazed onto a steel body because carbide holds an edge far longer than high-speed steel in abrasive hardwoods and manufactured boards. Many profile bits also carry a small ball-bearing pilot at the tip or above the cutter; this bearing rides against the edge of the workpiece and controls how deep the profile bites, so the bit follows the board's own edge or a template without a separate fence.

Bits fall into recognisable groups. Straight bits cut square-bottomed grooves, dados, and rabbets and are the workhorses of joinery. Round-over and ogee bits soften or decorate edges. Flush-trim and pattern bits carry a bearing the same diameter as the cutter so they copy a template or trim one surface even with another, which is the basis of template routing. Chamfer bits cut angled bevels. Cove bits cut a concave quarter-circle. Rabbeting bits cut a stepped shoulder, often with interchangeable bearings to vary the width. Specialised bits cut dovetails, finger joints, raised panels, and tongue-and-groove profiles.

Two practical points govern bit selection. First, shank size: buy half-inch-shank bits wherever a bit is offered in both sizes, because the thicker shank flexes less and cuts more cleanly, especially on large-diameter profile bits. Second, cleanliness and sharpness: a dull or resin-clogged bit burns the wood, tears the grain, and forces you to push harder, which is both a quality problem and a safety hazard. Bits should be wiped clean of pitch, stored so their edges do not knock together, and either resharpened by a professional or replaced when they stop slicing cleanly.

The geometry of a straight bit's flutes matters more than beginners expect. A standard straight bit has flutes parallel to the shank and simply plunges and cuts, but spiral bits twist their cutting edges like a drill, which shears the wood more cleanly and clears chips efficiently. An up-cut spiral pulls chips up and out of the cut, keeping a deep mortise clear, but it can lift and splinter the top surface. A down-cut spiral presses chips down, leaving a crisp top edge, which is prized for cutting sheet goods and veneered panels without chipping the face, though it clears chips less well from a deep slot. Compression bits combine both, cutting up at the tip and down at the top to leave both faces clean. Choosing flute geometry to suit the material and the cut is an advanced habit that markedly improves results.

sections.heading: Setting Cut Depth Safely
sections.body:
Depth of cut is the single most important setting on a router, and getting it wrong is the most common cause of both ruined work and dangerous kickback. The rule that experienced woodworkers follow is simple: take shallow passes. Trying to remove a deep profile or a full-depth groove in one pass forces the bit to chew through too much material at once, which bogs the motor, burns the wood, tears the grain, and can wrench the tool out of your control. Instead, set a modest depth, make a pass, then lower the bit a few millimetres and pass again, repeating until you reach the final depth. A general guideline is to remove no more than about three millimetres of depth per pass with a straight bit, and less with a large-diameter profile bit.

On a fixed-base router you set depth by loosening a clamp and either turning the motor in a threaded housing or sliding it up or down against a scale, then locking it. On a plunge router you set the final depth with an adjustable stop rod that bottoms against a turret of stepped stops; the turret lets you preset two or three intermediate depths so you can step down to full depth quickly and repeatably. Always confirm the setting on scrap of the same thickness before touching the real workpiece.

A subtle but vital safety habit is to check that the bit is not set so deep that it can strike the bench, a clamp, or a screw hidden in the wood. Before switching on, spin the collet by hand to be sure the bit turns freely and the depth stop is engaged. When the tool is running, never adjust depth; switch off, wait for the bit to stop completely, and only then change the setting. Treating depth as something you build up in stages, rather than achieve in one bite, is the mark of safe router work.

A reliable way to set an exact final depth is to zero the bit against the surface first. With the router unplugged, lower the bit until it just touches the workpiece or a known reference, then set your scale or plunge stop to zero and dial in the depth you want from there. For repeat setups, keeping a set of setup blocks or gauge bars of known thickness lets you set the same depth every time without measuring. On a plunge router the stepped turret is invaluable: preset the tallest stop to a shallow first pass, the middle to an intermediate, and the shortest to full depth, and you can step down through the passes simply by rotating the turret between them, which makes repeatable multi-pass cuts fast and foolproof.

sections.heading: Feed Direction and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Feed direction — the way you move the router relative to the spinning bit — is a concept beginners often overlook and then learn the hard way. The bit spins clockwise when you look down at a handheld router from above. For the cutter to pull itself into the wood in a controlled way and for the tool to want to stay against the workpiece, you must feed the router so that the cutting edge meets fresh wood in opposition to your travel. In practical terms, when routing the outside edge of a workpiece with a handheld router, you move the tool from left to right, so the router travels counter-clockwise around the outside of the piece. When routing the inside of a frame or an opening, the direction reverses: you go clockwise.

Feeding the correct way is called a conventional cut, and it gives you a smooth, controllable cut where the tool naturally hugs the edge. Feeding the wrong way produces a climb cut, in which the bit's rotation grabs the wood and tries to run the router along the cut faster than you intend. A climb cut can be useful in specific, controlled situations to avoid tear-out on difficult grain, but for a beginner and for any freehand work it is dangerous, because the tool can lunge sideways out of your grip.

The same logic applies in reverse at a router table, where the bit is mounted upside down and spins counter-clockwise as you look at it from the operator's side. There you feed the workpiece from right to left, against the rotation. A useful memory aid is that the wood should always be fed so the cutter pushes against your feed, not with it. Before every cut, pause and picture which way the bit turns and which way fresh wood should meet it; making this a habit prevents the most alarming surprises the tool can deliver.

There is one common situation where a deliberate, controlled climb cut is the right choice: a light final skim pass to eliminate tear-out on figured grain. Because a climb cut compresses the fibres against the workpiece rather than lifting them, a shallow climbing pass can leave a glass-smooth surface where a conventional cut would splinter. The key words are light and controlled: the pass must remove only a whisper of material, both hands must have a firm grip, and the router must be braced so the tool's tendency to run cannot pull it out of the cut. Beginners should master conventional feeding thoroughly before attempting climb cuts, and should never climb-cut freehand on a deep pass, where the tool can lunge unpredictably.

sections.heading: Edge Profiling and Decorative Mouldings
sections.body:
One of the most satisfying uses of a router is turning a plain square edge into a shaped profile: a soft round-over that is kinder to hands and less prone to chipping, a chamfered bevel, a classical ogee, a cove, or a bead. Edge profiling relies on a bearing-guided bit, where a ball-bearing pilot rides along the edge of the board and sets how far the cutter reaches in, so you do not need a separate fence for a straight edge. You simply guide the router along the workpiece, keeping the base flat and the bearing in firm contact with the edge.

Good results come from a few disciplines. Take the profile in two or three increasing passes rather than one, exactly as with depth of cut, because a full-depth profile bit removes a great deal of wood and will burn or tear if rushed. Move at a steady pace: too slow and friction scorches the wood, leaving brown burn marks that are tedious to sand out; too fast and the cut is rough and the motor labours. Keep the router moving continuously through the cut and off the end, because pausing in one place lets the bit dwell and burn.

End grain deserves special care, because it splinters as the bit exits the corner of a board. The standard trick when profiling all four edges of a rectangular top is to rout the two end-grain edges first and the two long-grain edges last; any tear-out at the corners of the end-grain cuts is then removed when the long-grain passes clean up the corners. A backer block clamped at the exit corner also supports the fibres and prevents blow-out. With these habits, a router transforms a workshop's output from plain boxes into pieces with crisp, professional edges.

Combining profiles multiplies what a router can do with a small set of bits. A round-over on the top edge and a cove beneath it produce a classical thumbnail moulding; a chamfer stacked with a bead gives a picture-frame look. You can also build a large moulding by making several passes with different bits along the same edge, shifting the fence or bit height between passes. When matching new moulding to existing trim, cut test pieces and hold them against the original in the same light, because a profile that looks right on the bench can read differently once it is installed and casting shadows. Keeping a labelled sample board of the profiles your bits produce, at the settings you used, saves rediscovering a good setup months later.

sections.heading: Grooves, Dados, and Rabbets
sections.body:
Beyond decorative edges, a router is a precise joinery tool for cutting the channels that hold shelves, panels, and drawer bottoms. A groove runs with the grain; a dado runs across it; a rabbet is a stepped recess cut along an edge or end. All three are the structural backbone of casework, because a shelf seated in a dado is far stronger and easier to assemble square than one simply screwed to a face.

Straight bits cut these features, and the key to accuracy is guiding the router in a dead-straight line at a consistent distance from a reference. For a rabbet along an edge you can use a rabbeting bit with a bearing, which needs no fence. For a groove or dado away from the edge you guide the router against a straightedge clamped to the work, or against the tool's own edge guide — an adjustable fence that bolts to the base and rides along the board's edge. Measure the offset between the bit and the base edge carefully, because the router references the base, not the bit, and a small error is doubled if you cut from the wrong side of your line.

Width and depth both matter for a joint that fits. A dado sized to the exact thickness of a modern plywood shelf is a common frustration, because plywood is almost always thinner than its nominal size; special undersized straight bits exist to match real plywood thicknesses, or you cut the dado in two passes, shifting the fence slightly for the second. Cut depth to about a third to a half of the board's thickness for a strong housing. As always, reach final depth in stages, test the fit in scrap first, and label which face rode against the fence so every matching cut references the same surface.

Stopped versions of these joints — where the channel does not run all the way to the edge, so it stays hidden on an assembled piece — are where a plunge router earns its place. To cut a stopped dado, mark where the groove must begin and end, clamp a straightedge, plunge the bit at the start mark, travel to the end mark, and retract; the rounded ends the bit leaves are either squared with a chisel or matched by rounding the corners of the shelf that fits them. For through joints, clamping a sacrificial backer board tight against the exit edge prevents the blow-out that otherwise splinters the back corner as the bit breaks through. Dry-fitting every joint before glue-up, and numbering the parts so each returns to the cut that fits it, turns router joinery into reliably square casework.

sections.heading: Template and Pattern Routing
sections.body:
Template routing is the technique that lets a router reproduce a shape exactly, again and again, and it is what makes the tool indispensable for curved and repeated parts. The method uses a flush-trim or pattern bit whose guide bearing is the same diameter as the cutter. You fix a template — a piece of hardboard, plywood, or acrylic cut precisely to the shape you want — on top of or beneath the workpiece, and run the router so the bearing rides along the template's edge while the cutter trims the workpiece to match. Because the bearing and cutter share a diameter, the workpiece ends up identical to the template.

The difference between a flush-trim bit and a pattern bit is only where the bearing sits: a flush-trim bit has the bearing at the tip, below the cutter, so the template goes underneath the work; a pattern bit has the bearing at the top of the cutter, so the template sits on top. Owning both, or a bit with bearings that can be moved, lets you always keep the template on the convenient side and reverse direction to suit the grain, which matters because routing against difficult grain tears out.

The workflow rewards preparation. First rough-cut the workpiece with a jigsaw or bandsaw to within a few millimetres of the final line, so the router only has to trim a thin sliver rather than hog off a wide margin; asking a bearing bit to remove too much at once invites burning and a bit that grabs. Attach the template firmly with double-sided tape, screws in waste areas, or toggle clamps, because any shift ruins the copy. For production runs — chair parts, brackets, curved rails — one well-made template turns a router into a small factory, producing dozens of parts that are indistinguishable from one another.

Making a good template is itself a skill worth developing, because the router copies every flaw as faithfully as every virtue. Cut the template slightly oversize, then refine its edge with sandpaper, a file, or a spokeshave until the curve is fair and free of bumps, sighting along it in raking light where imperfections show. Hardboard and plywood make cheap templates; clear acrylic lets you see the workpiece and the grain beneath, which helps you position the template to avoid tear-out. For parts that will be routed many times, a template of a durable material with the bearing surface sealed and waxed lasts longer and slides more smoothly. When the grain direction reverses around a curved template, plan to rout each portion in the direction that cuts downhill into the grain, flipping the workpiece or using a bit with movable bearings so you never have to force a cut against the grain.

sections.heading: The Router Table
sections.body:
Mounting a router upside down beneath a flat table transforms how the tool is used and, for many operations, makes it safer and more accurate. In a router table the motor hangs below the surface with the bit projecting up through a hole, and instead of moving the tool across the work, you move the work across the tool. A fence sets the depth of cut for straight work, and the table's flat surface guarantees the base is always dead flat, which is hard to maintain freehand on small or narrow pieces.

The router table shines for several jobs. Narrow stock — a thin strip that a handheld router would tip off — is fully supported on a table. Small parts that would be dangerous to hold under a handheld router are pushed past the bit with a push block. Bits too large to use safely by hand, such as raised-panel cutters, are meant to be run only in a table, where the fence and the mass of the table steady the cut. Repetitive profiling of many identical edges is faster and more consistent, because the setting stays fixed and you simply feed part after part.

A functional table needs a few features: a flat top, a straight and adjustable fence with a gap that closes around the bit to support the wood right up to the cut, and a way to raise and lower the bit precisely — many routers offer above-table height adjustment for exactly this. Feed direction on a table is right to left, against the bit's rotation, the mirror image of handheld work. Guards, a bit guard over the cutter, and featherboards that hold the stock against the fence and down on the table all make the table both safer and more accurate, and no serious router table should be run without them.

Featherboards and push blocks are not optional extras on a router table; they are what make it the safe way to run cuts that would be dangerous freehand. A featherboard is a comb of angled fingers clamped to the fence or table that presses the workpiece firmly against the fence or down onto the table and, crucially, resists kickback by allowing the wood to move only forward. A push block or push stick keeps your hands well away from the bit at the end of a cut, where fingers would otherwise pass closest to the cutter. Starting pins and bit guards further reduce risk when shaping curved parts against a bearing. Setting these up for every cut, rather than only when a piece feels risky, builds the habit that prevents the moment of inattention that causes injuries.

sections.heading: Choosing Bit Speed for Diameter
sections.body:
A router's cutting speed at the edge of the bit depends on both the motor's revolutions per minute and the diameter of the bit, and matching speed to diameter is a genuine safety and quality issue that beginners routinely ignore. The rim of a large bit travels much faster than the rim of a small one at the same rpm, because it has farther to go around. A small quarter-inch straight bit run at full speed cuts cleanly, but a large three-inch raised-panel bit run at that same full speed has a rim velocity so high that it can burn the wood, stress the bit, and become genuinely dangerous.

For this reason many routers offer variable speed, and the rule is to slow the motor down as bit diameter goes up. As a rough guide, bits up to about an inch in diameter can run at full speed, around twenty-two to twenty-four thousand rpm; bits between one and two inches should be dropped to roughly eighteen thousand rpm; bits between two and two and a half inches to around sixteen thousand; and the largest panel-raising bits over three inches down to twelve thousand rpm or lower. Manufacturers usually print a maximum safe rpm on the bit or its packaging, and that figure should never be exceeded.

Slower speed on a big bit does not mean a rougher cut. Because the large rim is still moving quickly in absolute terms, a reduced rpm gives a clean surface while keeping rim velocity, heat, and stress within safe bounds. If your router has only a single high speed, large-diameter bits should simply not be used in it; they belong in a variable-speed router mounted in a table. Learning to think about rim speed rather than just rpm is part of graduating from a beginner to a confident router user.

Rim speed, the number that actually matters, is the bit's circumference multiplied by its revolutions, and it climbs steeply with diameter. This is why a three-inch panel-raising bit at full router speed has a rim moving fast enough to be genuinely hazardous and to scorch wood on contact, while the same rpm on a quarter-inch bit is perfectly safe. Beyond respecting the printed maximum, listen and watch: a bit run too fast for its size squeals and burns, while one run at the right speed cuts with a steady sound and throws clean chips. Large bits also demand that the workpiece be fed more slowly and that passes be lighter, because each cutting edge is removing a longer arc of material. Treating a big bit with the caution its rim speed deserves is one of the clearest markers of an experienced router user.

sections.heading: Preventing Tear-Out and Burn Marks
sections.body:
Two defects spoil more router work than any others: tear-out, where the grain lifts and splinters instead of shearing cleanly, and burn marks, where friction scorches the wood brown.
