Both are preventable once you understand their causes. Tear-out happens when the bit cuts against the grain and levers fibres up rather than slicing them. It is worst at the exit corners of a cut and on figured or interlocked grain. The remedies are to cut end grain before long grain when profiling all four edges, to use a backer block that supports fibres where the bit exits, to take light passes so the bit shears rather than tears, and, on stubborn grain, to make a light controlled climb cut for the final pass so the bit compresses the fibres against the workpiece.

Burn marks come from heat, and heat comes from the bit dwelling too long in one place or from a dull or dirty bit. A sharp, clean bit slices and throws chips that carry heat away; a dull one rubs and scorches. So the first defence against burning is a sharp bit, wiped free of pitch. The second is to keep the router moving steadily and never pause mid-cut, especially on curves and at the ends of a pass where it is tempting to slow down. The third is to take a final very light pass that skims off any burned surface.

Feed rate ties both defects together. Too slow invites burning; too fast invites tear-out and overloads the motor. The right pace is a steady, deliberate walk that keeps chips flowing and the motor humming rather than straining. Listening to the motor and watching the chips — clean curls rather than fine dust — tells you whether the pace is right. With a sharp bit, light passes, correct feed direction, and steady motion, most router work comes off the tool needing only light sanding.

Wood species and grain figure change how much care each defect demands. Straight-grained softwoods and mild hardwoods like poplar rout cleanly with ordinary care, while highly figured woods — curly maple, birdseye, interlocked tropical grain — tear out readily because the grain direction reverses within a single pass. On such woods, lighter passes, sharper bits, a backer for support, and a controlled climbing skim for the final pass all become more important. Resinous woods such as pine burn and clog bits faster, so they reward a keen edge and a brisk feed. Sealing the cut surface is not possible before routing, but knowing that a particular board will be difficult lets you slow down, test on an offcut of the same stock, and adjust technique before committing to the finished piece.

sections.heading: Freehand Routing, Signs, and Inlay
sections.body:
Not all router work follows a fence or a template. Freehand routing — guiding the tool by eye — lets you carve lettering into a sign, hollow a shallow relief, or clear the waste inside an irregular shape. It demands the most control of any router technique, because nothing but your hands keeps the bit on the line, so it is where the disciplines of sharp bits, light passes, and correct feed direction matter most. A plunge router is almost always used, so the bit can be dropped into the interior and lifted out cleanly, and small trim routers are popular for freehand work because their light weight and one-handed grip give fine control.

Sign carving is the classic freehand job. Letters are laid out on the board, a small straight or V-groove bit is set to a shallow depth, and the router is walked along each stroke of each letter. V-groove and core-box bits give lettering a carved, three-dimensional look because they cut a valley whose width grows with depth, so you control line weight by plunge depth. Because a slip shows permanently, most sign carvers practise on scrap, work in good light, and take the depth in two passes.

Inlay work uses the router to cut a shallow recess that exactly matches a decorative piece — a contrasting wood, a metal strip, or a manufactured inlay band — which is then glued flush into the recess. Specialised inlay kits pair a small bit with a template guide bushing and a removable collar, so the same template cuts both the recess and the inlay to matching sizes with a built-in allowance for the glue line. Freehand and inlay routing reward patience, and they are where the tool crosses from carpentry into craft.

A useful halfway house between fully freehand work and a rigid template is a guide that constrains the router in just one axis while leaving you free in the other. A simple fence lets you rout a straight line freehand along its length; a trammel arm pins the router to a centre and lets you swing perfect arcs and circles for clock faces, table tops, and curved rails. For lettering, printed or traced templates combined with a guide bushing turn sign-making from a nerve-racking freehand exercise into a repeatable, accurate process. Whatever the aid, freehand and semi-freehand routing reward a slow, deliberate pace and good lighting, because the router removes material permanently and a wandering line cannot be un-cut. Practising the path with the motor off, walking the tool through the whole cut before switching on, builds the muscle memory that keeps the bit on the line.

sections.heading: Guide Bushings, Fences, and Jigs
sections.body:
Accuracy in routing usually comes not from a steady hand but from a jig or a guide that removes the chance of error, and learning to make and use these accessories is what separates rough work from precise work. The simplest guide is a straightedge clamped to the workpiece; the router base rides along it to cut a dead-straight groove or trim a panel to a line. The tool's own edge guide, an adjustable fence bolted to the base, does the same job referenced from the board's edge, and it is the standard way to cut a groove a set distance in from an edge.

Guide bushings, also called template guide bushings, are metal collars that mount in the router base concentric with the bit and project below it. Running the collar against a template lets the router follow the template while the bit cuts a path offset from it by the difference between the collar and bit diameters. This offset must be accounted for when the template is made, and it is the basis of hinge-mortising jigs, dovetail jigs, and lettering templates. Unlike a bearing-guided bit, a bushing works with any straight bit and does not require the template and workpiece to be the same size.

Purpose-built jigs handle the jobs that come up repeatedly. A dovetail jig clamps two boards and, with a guide bushing and a dovetail bit, cuts interlocking pins and tails for drawers in a fraction of the time hand-cutting takes. A mortising jig positions the router for consistent mortises. Circle-cutting jigs pivot the router around a centre pin to rout perfect discs and arcs. Box-joint jigs index evenly spaced fingers. Many woodworkers build their own jigs from scrap for one-off tasks, and the habit of asking "what jig would make this cut foolproof?" is central to getting the most from a router.

The offset a guide bushing introduces between the template edge and the cut is not a nuisance to be tolerated but a dimension to be exploited. Because the bit cuts a path offset inward from the collar by half the difference of their diameters, a single template can cut both halves of a mating joint — a recess and the piece that fills it — simply by routing one from above and one from below, or by swapping collar sizes, with the offset providing the clearance for a glue line. Inlay kits formalise this with a collar and a removable sleeve sized so the recess and the inlay differ by exactly the right amount for a snug fit. Understanding and deliberately calculating the bushing offset, rather than being surprised by it, unlocks a whole class of precise, repeatable joinery that would be nearly impossible to cut by hand.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Care, and Safe Habits
sections.body:
A router is a durable tool, but it rewards basic care and punishes neglect. The collet deserves the most attention, because it is what keeps the bit from working loose at twenty thousand revolutions per minute. Keep it clean of pitch and dust, seat the bit fully and then withdraw it a small amount before tightening so the bit does not bottom out against the shaft, and tighten firmly with the wrench rather than by hand. A worn or corroded collet no longer grips reliably and should be replaced. Never run a bit with the shank only partly inserted, because it can vibrate loose and become a projectile.

The motor needs airflow and clean brushes. Keep the cooling vents clear of dust so the motor does not overheat, and on brushed motors inspect and replace the carbon brushes when they wear down, which restores a motor that has begun to run weakly or spark excessively. Bits should be stored so their edges do not knock together, wiped clean of resin after use, and kept sharp; a dull bit is both a quality and a safety problem.

Safe habits tie all of this together. Always unplug the router before changing a bit or a base, because an accidental start with your fingers at the collet is catastrophic. Wear eye protection against flung chips and hearing protection against the shriek of the motor, and a dust mask against fine wood dust. Clamp the workpiece so both hands are free to control the tool. Let the motor reach full speed before entering the cut and let the bit stop completely before setting the tool down, since a spinning bit set on a bench will walk the router off it. Keep hands well clear of the bit's path and never reach under a running router. These habits, practised until they are automatic, are what let a woodworker use this powerful tool for decades without injury.

Vibration and noise are diagnostic as well as nuisances. A router that suddenly vibrates more than usual may have a bent bit, a bit not seated fully in the collet, a worn collet that no longer grips concentrically, or accumulated pitch throwing the bit off balance; each is a reason to stop, unplug, and investigate rather than push on. A motor that sparks heavily or runs weak often needs new brushes. Beyond the machine, the workshop habits that keep routing safe are worth stating plainly: keep the cord clear of the bit's path so it cannot be cut, never wear loose sleeves or gloves that a spinning bit could catch, keep bystanders out of the line the tool would travel in a kickback, and always give the router your full attention, because it is unforgiving of the moment of distraction that most tools would tolerate.

guides.safetyNote: A router spins a sharp bit at up to twenty-four thousand revolutions per minute and is one of the most dangerous tools in a workshop. Always unplug it before changing a bit or base, wear eye and hearing protection and a dust mask, clamp the work so both hands control the tool, feed against the bit's rotation, take light passes, match bit speed to bit diameter, and let the bit stop completely before setting the tool down. This guide is general information, not a substitute for the tool's own manual or hands-on instruction.

guides.title: Choosing and Using an Angle Grinder
guides.summary: How to pick the right angle grinder and discs for metal, masonry, and tile work, mount wheels correctly, grind and cut with safe technique, avoid kickback and disc failure, and manage the sparks, dust, and fire risks that come with the tool.
guides.safetyNote: An angle grinder spins an abrasive wheel at around 80 meters per second at the rim, and it is among the most injury-prone tools in any workshop: wheels can shatter, the tool can kick back toward your body, and the spark stream can start fires long after you stop work. Always use the guard and side handle, wear impact-rated eye protection plus a face shield, hearing protection, gloves, and snug clothing, and never fit a disc rated below the tool's spindle speed or use a cutting disc for side grinding. Unplug or remove the battery before changing discs, keep bystanders and flammables well clear, check the work area for smoldering material for at least half an hour after sparking work, and wear a proper respirator when cutting masonry or concrete, because the silica dust is a serious lung hazard. This guide is general education — the manuals for your specific grinder and discs take precedence.

sections.heading: What an Angle Grinder Is and What It Can Do
sections.body:
An angle grinder — also called a disc grinder or side grinder — is a handheld power tool that spins an abrasive disc at very high speed on a spindle set at a right angle to the motor. That geometry is the meaning of the word angle in the name: the motor lies along the body where your hand grips, and a gear head turns the drive ninety degrees so the disc faces sideways, letting you press its face or edge against the work. The concept dates to the early twentieth century; the German company Ackermann + Schmitt, later known as FLEX, produced an early portable grinder in 1954 that was so identified with the type that Germans still commonly call any angle grinder a Flex and use flexen as a verb meaning to cut with one. Today every major tool brand makes them, from disposable-cheap to industrial, and they are as ordinary on job sites as drills.

What makes the angle grinder worth a place in a home workshop is its breadth. With the right disc, one tool grinds welds flat, cuts rusted bolts and rebar, slices steel pipe and angle iron, removes rust and paint, sharpens lawnmower blades and axes, cuts ceramic tile and pavers, chases grooves in brick and concrete, shapes stone, strips mortar from old brick for repointing, and sands curved wood. Very few tools convert between materials as different as hardened steel and granite by nothing more than a disc change. The flip side of that versatility is that the grinder has no table, no fence, no blade brake on most models, and no automatic sense of what it is touching: it is a raw rotating force that you aim entirely by hand, which is why technique and respect occupy so much of this guide.

It helps to understand how the tool removes material, because it explains both its power and its dangers. An abrasive disc is not a blade with teeth; it is a matrix of hard mineral grains — aluminum oxide, zirconia, silicon carbide, ceramic, or industrial diamond — bonded together with resin or metal. Each grain is a microscopic cutting tooth, and the disc works by dragging millions of them across the work per second, each tearing away a tiny chip. As grains dull, they fracture or tear free, exposing fresh sharp grains beneath — the disc is designed to consume itself. That self-sacrifice is why grinding produces the signature stream of sparks (incandescent steel chips mixed with burning abrasive), why discs shrink with use, and why disc quality and condition matter so much: the bond holding those grains is all that stands between a working wheel and a cloud of fragments moving at highway speed.

The rim speed deserves a number early, because everything in the safety sections follows from it. A common 4.5-inch (115 mm) grinder spins at 10,000 to 11,000 revolutions per minute unloaded, which puts the rim of the disc at roughly 80 meters per second — about 180 miles per hour. Nothing else in a home shop moves a consumable that fast that close to your hands and face. Treat the grinder as the most serious tool you own, learn it deliberately, and it will replace a shed full of single-purpose equipment; treat it casually and it is, by the injury statistics of every country that keeps them, one of the likeliest tools to put its user in an emergency department.

sections.heading: Sizes, Power, and Speed: Choosing the Right Grinder
sections.body:
Angle grinders are sized by the largest disc they accept, and the size decision is the most consequential one you make at purchase. The overwhelmingly most useful size for home and general repair work is the small grinder taking 4.5-inch (115 mm) discs, with its close sibling the 5-inch (125 mm) — many models accept both. These small grinders are light (typically 4 to 6 pounds), controllable with one hand steadying and one guiding, spin at 10,000 to 11,500 rpm, and take the widest, cheapest selection of discs on the market. At the other end stand the large 7-inch and 9-inch (180 and 230 mm) machines: far more powerful, turning slower (around 6,000 to 6,600 rpm, because rim speed limits scale with diameter), heavy enough to demand two committed hands, and capable of deep cuts in masonry and heavy steel. They are also disproportionately dangerous — a 9-inch grinder's torque makes its kickback nearly unstoppable, and some industrial sites ban them outright in favor of smaller machines. A first grinder should be a 4.5 or 5-inch; buy bigger only when a specific recurring job demands it, and consider renting for one-off heavy work.

Power ratings tell you how hard you can lean on the tool before it bogs. Corded small grinders run from budget 6-amp motors (around 700 watts) to 13-amp (about 1,500 watts) professional models; in the middle, 9 to 11 amps is a sweet spot for home use — enough not to stall in a deep cut, not so much torque that the tool fights you. Corded tools remain excellent value: simple, light for their power, and immune to dead batteries. Cordless grinders on modern 18-volt and higher platforms have closed most of the performance gap and are now the default on many job sites for their freedom from a trailing cord — a real safety benefit, since cords near spinning discs and spark streams are a hazard of their own. Their costs are weight (battery packs add a pound or more), price, and runtime: grinding is among the hungriest tasks a battery faces. If you already own tools on a battery platform, the matching grinder is usually the sensible pick; if this is your first serious power tool, a mid-range corded model gives the most capability per dollar.

Speed and its control separate basic tools from better ones. Fixed single-speed models suit most metalwork, since abrasives for metal are designed for full speed. Variable-speed grinders earn their premium if you plan to polish, sand wood, or work with wire wheels and flap discs on delicate material, where slower rim speeds prevent burning and unloading. Whatever the speed, the number printed on the tool — its maximum unloaded rpm — is a hard limit that every accessory must meet or exceed, a rule the disc section returns to with emphasis.

The features genuinely worth paying for are safety features. A paddle switch (dead-man switch) that stops the tool the instant your grip relaxes is the single most valuable; contrast it with slide switches that lock on and keep the disc spinning after the tool leaves your hand or you leave the tool. Electronic restart protection prevents the grinder from bursting back to life when power returns after an outage or a tripped breaker with the switch still locked on. A mechanical brake that halts the disc in a second or two rather than letting it freewheel for ten is a major hand-saver. Soft start tames the twist the motor gives at switch-on; an anti-kickback clutch or electronic kickback stop disengages drive when the disc jams; a tool-free adjustable guard encourages you to actually keep the guard positioned correctly; and a vibration-damped side handle makes the two-handed grip — mandatory, as later sections insist — comfortable enough that you keep it. On a tool this fast, those features are not conveniences; they are the difference between an incident and an injury.

sections.heading: Understanding Discs: Grinding Wheels, Cutting Discs, Flap Discs, and Wire Wheels
sections.body:
The grinder is only half the tool; the disc is the working half, and the families of discs are worth knowing individually because each is engineered for one kind of force and can fail violently under another. The first family is the depressed-center grinding wheel (Type 27 in American nomenclature), the classic thick wheel — typically about a quarter-inch (6 mm) thick — made of abrasive grain in a resinoid bond, reinforced with layers of fiberglass mesh. Its job is stock removal using the face of the wheel at a shallow angle: flattening welds, beveling edges for welding, grinding rust pits, notching steel. The depressed center lets the mounting hardware sit below the working face so the wheel can grind flat surfaces. These wheels are consumed steadily in use and are the workhorse for rough metal shaping.

The second family is the cut-off wheel: a thin flat or depressed-center disc, from a full eighth of an inch down to 1 mm, also resin-bonded and fiberglass-reinforced. Thin wheels cut fast, cool, and with a narrow kerf — a 1 mm disc slices bolt shanks and sheet steel with startling ease — but their thinness is exactly why the cardinal rule of this whole guide exists: a cutting disc must only ever be loaded in its plane. Used edge-on it is strong; pressed sideways, twisted in the cut, or used for grinding on its flat face, it snaps, and a snapped disc at 80 meters per second becomes shrapnel. The prohibition on side-grinding with cut-off wheels is printed on every disc and appears in every abrasive-industry safety code; it is the most-violated and most consequential rule in amateur grinder use.

The third family, the flap disc, has largely conquered finish work. Instead of a solid abrasive mass, overlapping flaps of abrasive cloth are glued radially to a backing plate; as flaps wear they shed, exposing fresh grain. Flap discs grind and blend in one step — removing a weld and leaving a near-finished surface — run smoother with less gouging and less vibration than hard wheels, and come in grits from 40 (aggressive) through 60 and 80 to 120 (fine). For most home metalwork short of heavy stock removal, a 60- or 80-grit zirconia flap disc is the most pleasant disc in the kit. Related coated products include sanding discs on rubber backing pads and paint-and-rust stripping discs of open nylon web impregnated with abrasive, which shear off coatings without deeply scoring the metal beneath.

The fourth family is wire: cup brushes and wheel brushes of crimped or twisted-knot steel strands, for stripping rust, scale, old paint, and weld spatter. Knotted wire is aggressive; crimped is gentler. Wire tools have a specific hazard profile: individual wires fatigue, break, and fly off constantly in use — they can bury themselves in skin and stick in clothing — so a face shield and genuinely thick clothing matter more here than with any other disc, and the tool's rpm limit matters absolutely, because an over-sped brush sheds wires in showers. Run wire brushes so the wire tips do the work with light pressure; jamming them bends wires and accelerates shedding.

The fifth family is the diamond blade for masonry and tile, covered in depth in the next section, and beside these five stand specialty items — semi-flexible discs for stone, felt and foam polishing pads used with compounds, rubber backing pads, and, sold widely but deserving of a hard warning, toothed wood-carving discs. Chainsaw-tooth and multi-tooth carving wheels convert the grinder into a tool that grabs; abrasive discs slip when overloaded, but teeth bite and climb, and the injury record of chainsaw discs on angle grinders is grim enough that several safety authorities advise against them for non-specialists. If you carve wood with a grinder, choose surface-abrasive carving discs over toothed ones, use the guard and both hands, and treat the tool with chainsaw-grade respect.

sections.heading: Matching the Disc to the Material: Metal, Masonry, Tile, and Stainless
sections.body:
Every disc is a chemistry choice as much as a shape choice, and matching abrasive to material is the difference between fast clean work and glazed, overheating frustration — or a broken wheel. For ordinary carbon steel — the angle iron, rebar, pipe, and mild plate of most repair work — the default abrasives are aluminum oxide, the brown-gray standard grain, and zirconia alumina, a tougher blue-green grain that cuts faster and lasts longer under pressure. Premium ceramic alumina grains cut cooler and faster still and are worth their price for heavy or frequent work. All three are sold in grinding wheels, cut-off discs, and flap discs; for occasional home use, mid-grade zirconia products hit the value point.

Stainless steel adds a contamination rule that surprises newcomers. Discs for stainless are labeled INOX (the European term) and are manufactured with negligible iron, sulfur, and chlorine content, because ordinary discs embed free iron and contaminants into the stainless surface, which later bloom as rust stains and can compromise corrosion resistance; the sulfur and chlorine limits matter for weld integrity in critical work. The contamination travels both ways: a disc that has ground carbon steel will transfer iron to stainless afterward, so careful fabricators dedicate discs (and even grinders) to stainless only. For home projects — a stainless rail, a sink repair — buy INOX-marked discs, keep them for stainless, and grind gently, because stainless work-hardens: high pressure and heat make the surface harder and bluer as you fight it. Aluminum and other soft metals pose the opposite problem: they load the wheel, smearing into its pores until the face glazes and skates, and a heavily loaded wheel runs out of balance. Special aluminum-rated discs resist loading; rubbing the disc periodically or lubricating with wax helps; and flap discs generally handle aluminum better than hard wheels.

Masonry — concrete, brick, block, stone, mortar — calls for entirely different abrasives, because silicate materials dull aluminum oxide almost instantly. The traditional answer is the silicon carbide masonry wheel, cheap and serviceable for occasional cuts; the modern answer is the diamond blade, a steel disc whose rim carries industrial diamond grit in a metal bond. Diamond blades outlast abrasive masonry discs many times over, cut faster, and hold their diameter (an abrasive disc shrinks as it wears, changing your depth of cut). Rim styles map to jobs: segmented rims — the rim divided by slots called gullets — clear dust and run coolest, cutting fastest but chipping the cut edge, right for concrete, pavers, and block; continuous-rim blades cut slowest and cleanest, the choice for ceramic and porcelain tile and for stone where edge quality matters; turbo rims, with a serrated continuous band, split the difference. Most home-duty diamond blades are dry-cutting rated, but even they benefit from cooling pauses; and any masonry cutting raises the crystalline silica dust problem, serious enough that this guide gives it a full section later — the short version is that a proper respirator or wet method is not optional.

Two matching rules stand above the details. First, never cut or grind a material the disc is not rated for: metal discs on masonry glaze and dull; masonry discs on metal can load, overheat, and break; and a standard diamond masonry blade used freehand on steel can overheat, lose segments, or snatch (metal-rated diamond wheels exist and are excellent, but the rating must say so). Wood is not a grinding material at all except with purpose-made carving discs — a standard abrasive wheel pressed into wood burns it and can grab. Second, when in doubt, read the disc: every legitimate wheel prints its material rating, its type, its maximum rpm, and its restrictions on its own label. The next section teaches how to read all of it, because that label is the manufacturer telling you exactly how not to be hurt by their product.

sections.heading: Reading a Disc's Markings: Speed Ratings, Expiry Dates, and Standards
sections.body:
Every reputable abrasive wheel carries a dense little block of print, and learning to read it takes five minutes that pay for the rest of your life. The single most important number is the maximum operating speed, given both as rpm and often as a rim speed in meters per second. The iron rule: the disc's maximum rpm must be equal to or greater than your grinder's no-load rpm. A 115 mm disc for small grinders is typically rated 13,300 rpm (80 m/s), safely above the 11,000 rpm of the tools it fits. The classic fatal error is mounting a larger disc on a smaller, faster tool — a 230 mm disc rated 6,600 rpm onto an 11,000 rpm small grinder (with the guard removed to make it fit, compounding the sin): the rim would be driven nearly double its design speed, and since centrifugal stress rises with the square of speed, the wheel is loaded toward four times its rated stress. Wheels burst under exactly this abuse, and the fragments carry rifle-order energy. Never up-size a disc, never remove a guard to make one fit, and never trust a disc whose speed marking is absent or illegible.

The label also declares the disc's identity and limits in standardized language. Look for the size line — outer diameter, thickness, and bore, such as 115 × 1.0 × 22.23 mm, that last figure being the near-universal 22.23 mm (7/8-inch) arbor of small grinders. Look for the type: Type 41 is a flat cut-off wheel, Type 42 a depressed-center cut-off wheel, Type 27 a depressed-center grinding wheel — and note that many jurisdictions and all manufacturers forbid side-grinding with Types 41 and 42, often printing not for side grinding explicitly. Look for the material rating (steel, INOX, stone, aluminum) and the abrasive specification code — a compact string like A60T-BF, decoding as aluminum oxide grain (A), grit 60, hardness grade T, resinoid bond fiberglass-reinforced (BF). Pictograms repeat the restrictions without words: a struck-through image of side grinding, mandatory eye protection, do not use if damaged, do not use freehand for certain wheels. European discs carry the EN 12413 standard mark for bonded abrasives (EN 13236 for superabrasives like diamond) and usually the oSa symbol, the voluntary Organization for the Safety of Abrasives certification; American discs reference ANSI B7.1, the long-standing U.S. safety code for abrasive wheels.

Resin-bonded wheels also expire, which surprises almost everyone. The phenolic resin bond absorbs moisture and slowly degrades, so under EN 12413 every resinoid cutting and grinding wheel is stamped with a use-by date — printed on the metal ring around the bore or on the label, typically three years from manufacture (often as a quarter and year, like V04/2027, or a plain date). An expired wheel may look perfect and still have a weakened bond; the standard's answer, and this guide's, is simple: check the ring before mounting, and discard expired wheels. Storage drives the same chemistry — keep discs flat, dry, indoors, and off concrete floors; a wheel stored damp in a shed for years is suspect regardless of its printed date. Diamond blades, metal-bonded, do not carry resin expiry dates, but their steel cores fatigue: inspect for cracks radiating from the gullets and for missing segments.

Finally, the label is only as good as the disc's condition, so pair reading with the ring test tradition and inspection. Before mounting any bonded wheel, look it over under good light for cracks, chips at the rim, delamination, and a wetted or swollen look; for larger plain wheels, the old ring test — suspend the wheel on a finger through the bore and tap it lightly with a screwdriver handle; a sound wheel rings faintly, a cracked one thuds dead — still has value, though small depressed-center wheels are hard to ring meaningfully, which makes visual inspection and provenance (bought decent, stored dry, not dropped) your real assurance. Any disc that has been dropped on a hard floor is a discard, however it looks: the crack that kills is the one you cannot see, and discs are cheap in exactly the way hands are not.

sections.heading: Guards, Handles, and Switches: The Safety Features That Matter
sections.body:
The wheel guard is the one component that stands between a disc failure and your body, and understanding what it does makes you far less likely to commit the commonest grinder sin of removing it. The guard's first job is fragment containment: when a wheel bursts — and bursts happen, from cracks, expiry, over-speeding, or side-loading — the guard catches or deflects the fragments that would otherwise fan out in the wheel's plane at rim speed. Its second job is directing the spark and debris stream away from you in normal work, and its third is putting steel between your fingers and an exposed arc of spinning abrasive. The guard covers half the wheel; your technique orients that covered half toward your body, so the open half faces the work. Every guard on a modern grinder rotates: loosen the clamp (tool-free lever on better models), turn the guard so that the closed side is between wheel and operator for the grip you are using, and clamp it firmly. It should never be able to rotate under a blow. Adjusting the guard for each job takes five seconds; the injury it exists to prevent is a fragment in the face or throat.

Guards are also job-specific, which people forget. The standard Type 27 guard suits grinding wheels and flap discs. Cutting work properly calls for a Type 1/41 cutting guard, which wraps further around and encloses both faces of the thin wheel at the top — many manufacturers sell it as an accessory, and some jurisdictions and all abrasive makers require it for cut-off work. Wire cup brushes and polishing pads sit too wide or too soft for a wheel guard and are used with the appropriate guard or per the manual. What is never correct is no guard at all: the excuses — access into a tight corner, better sightlines, the disc that only fits without it — are precisely the circumstances of most guard-removal injuries. If the guard truly prevents access, the answer is a different tool (a die grinder, a multi-tool, a hacksaw), not an unguarded grinder.

The side handle is the other neglected safeguard. It threads into the head at either side (and often on top), and it converts the grinder from a one-handed wand into a two-handed tool you can actually hold against a kickback. Torque reaction when a disc jams arrives in a few milliseconds, far faster than reflex; the only grip that resists it is the one already in place — one hand on the body switch grip, the other on the side handle, thumbs and fingers wrapped, tool held so a kick rotates it away from your body line. Use the handle position that lets you do that for the cut at hand, and if you find yourself removing the handle to fit somewhere, apply the guard rule: wrong tool for the space. Anti-vibration handles are kinder to your hands in long sessions and reduce the numbing that degrades grip — relevant to the vibration white finger phenomenon that afflicts career grinder users.

Switches decide what the tool does in the worst second of a bad day. A paddle or dead-man switch stops the motor the instant your grip fails — dropped tool, kickback wrenching it loose, a stumble — while a locking slide switch keeps a dropped grinder running, skittering and climbing whatever it touches, including its own cord and your leg. For amateur use, the paddle switch with no lock-on, plus a brake that stops the wheel in a second or two, is the configuration to seek out; restart protection (the tool will not resume when power returns unless switched off and on) prevents the nasty surprise after a tripped breaker. Until the wheel has fully stopped, the grinder is not done: keep it in hand, wheel away from your body, and never set it down spinning — freewheeling discs walk tools off benches. Between jobs and for every disc change, kill the energy source entirely: unplug the cord or remove the battery, not merely switch off. A grinder that cannot start cannot hurt you while your fingers are on its spindle.

sections.heading: Personal Protective Equipment for Grinding Work
sections.body:
Grinding throws three things at your body continuously — high-velocity particles, noise, and dust — and occasionally a fourth, catastrophic one: fragments of a failed wheel. Dressing for the tool is therefore not gold-plating; it is the baseline the tool's own manual demands. Start with the eyes and face, the site of the most common grinder injuries. The correct standard is doubled protection: impact-rated safety glasses or goggles (ANSI Z87+ marked in the US, EN 166 with impact rating in Europe) worn under a full face shield. The glasses are the seal against fine particles that curl around a shield's edges; the shield spreads the load of larger strikes and protects the face, lips, and throat that glasses ignore. Wire-wheel work and cutting make the shield non-negotiable — broken wires and disc fragments aim for faces — and prescription wearers should know that ordinary eyeglasses are not impact-rated and shatter inward; wear rated over-glasses or goggles over them. Eye injuries from grinding are overwhelmingly from working bare-eyed or with glasses alone for just one quick cut; the particles do not know it was quick.

Hearing goes next, because grinders are loud in a damaging way: 95 to 105 decibels at the operator's ear is typical under load, well above the 85 dB threshold at which occupational rules require protection, and damage at those levels accumulates in minutes per day, permanently and painlessly. Foam plugs correctly inserted or quality earmuffs both work; muffs over plugs suit long sessions. Tinnitus — permanent ringing — is the classic grinder-user's souvenir, and it is entirely preventable at the cost of remembering the muffs that hang beside the tool.

Hands and body take the steady rain of sparks and the occasional grab. Wear snug-fitting leather or mechanics' gloves — snug matters, because loose gloves, like loose sleeves, drawstrings, scarves, and long hair, can wrap into a spinning spindle, and a grinder that catches fabric reels it in instantly. (This is also the argument against ever holding small work in one hand while grinding with the other: clamp the work, always, in a vise or with clamps to a bench — a grabbed workpiece either spins away as a projectile or drags the wheel across your holding hand.) Dress in flame-resistant or at least natural-fiber clothing — cotton, wool, leather aprons — never polyester fleece or other synthetics, which melt into skin when the spark stream lands and can smolder unnoticed; keep cuffs buttoned, shirts tucked, and pockets free of the tissues and lighter that spark streams find. Sturdy closed shoes handle the dropped-tool and hot-slag-on-floor cases. For long sessions, anti-vibration gloves take the edge off hand-arm vibration, which over years of heavy use causes the circulation damage called vibration white finger; at home-use exposure the risk is modest, but numb-tingling hands after a session are a signal to take breaks and let the tool's weight, not your squeeze, do the pressing.

Lungs, finally, and most under-respected: grinding metal makes fine metal and abrasive dust; grinding paint can volatilize lead on pre-1978 painted surfaces (test first — lead work needs containment and proper respirators, or a professional); and cutting concrete, brick, stone, or tile releases respirable crystalline silica, whose long-term inhalation causes silicosis, an incurable, progressive scarring of the lungs, along with elevated lung cancer risk. For general metal grinding, an N95/FFP2 disposable respirator is a sensible floor; for anything masonry, step up to a well-fitted half-mask respirator with P100/FFP3 filtration, and pair it with dust controls — wet cutting where the tool allows it, a shroud with HEPA vacuum extraction, or at minimum outdoor work positioned upwind. Occupational rules (OSHA's silica standard among them) treat uncontrolled dry masonry cutting as a serious violation for good reason; a weekend paver project deserves the same respect your lungs would be given on a job site.

sections.heading: Mounting a Disc Correctly
sections.body:
More grinder mishaps trace to careless disc changes than most users suspect: wheels cracked by over-tightening, flanges stacked wrong so the disc runs skewed, locking nuts left loose enough to let the disc spin on the spindle, and tools that started mid-change because the battery stayed in. The procedure below is generic; your manual's version governs where it differs.

Begin every change by removing the energy: unplug the cord, or remove the battery entirely — not just off. Then handle the hardware in order. The spindle carries an inner flange (a keyed washer that seats against the gear head), then the disc, then the outer flange nut that clamps it, tightened with the two-pin spanner supplied with the tool while the spindle-lock button holds the shaft. The two faces of the outer nut are different, and this is the detail most often botched: one side has a raised ring or recessed profile to fit through the bore of thin discs and clamp their flat, while the flipped side presents a flat or stepped face suited to thick depressed-center wheels — orient it so the nut clamps the disc's flat annulus around the bore without bearing on a raised hub or spanning a depression. A disc clamped on the wrong nut face runs wobbling or stressed and can crack at the bore. Press the spindle lock only with the wheel stopped — jamming it against a spinning or even coasting wheel shears the lock.

Inspect before you mount. Check the new disc's rating (correct diameter, bore, type for the guard fitted, rpm at or above the tool's, material right for the job, expiry date live) and its condition (no cracks, chips, delamination, moisture staining; never a dropped disc). Check the tool too: flanges clean and undamaged, spindle threads good, guard positioned for the work and clamped. Seat the disc concentric on the inner flange's pilot, spin the nut down by hand, then snug it with the pin spanner — firmly, but not with all your might; the wheel self-tightens slightly in use, and a gorilla-tight nut both stresses the disc and welds itself on for the next change. Hub-threaded wheels and backing-pad accessories thread straight onto the spindle without the nut; wire cups and some flap discs come in threaded (M14 or 5/8-11) versions for exactly this convenience.

After mounting, do what every abrasive standard requires and almost no amateur does: the test run. Stand aside — out of the wheel's plane — point the open side of the guard away from you and anyone else, and run the tool at full speed for thirty seconds to a minute. A flawed disc usually reveals itself immediately, by vibration, wobble, or failure, and the whole point of the test is that it does so while nobody is in the line of fire. Vibration that persists means stop: re-seat the disc, check the flanges, and if it still shakes, bin the disc. Thereafter, re-tension awareness continues in use — if a disc loosens, chatters, or the nut backs off, stop and re-mount — and at the session's end, loosen the nut while the tool is still warm if you struggled with it, store discs flat and dry, and leave the grinder with no disc mounted or the disc you would trust tomorrow.
steps: Unplug the grinder or remove its battery entirely before touching the spindle or disc.

Inspect the new disc: correct size, bore, and type; rpm rating at or above the tool's no-load speed; material rating for the job; unexpired date on resin wheels; no cracks, chips, or damage — and never use a disc that has been dropped.
Check the guard is the right type for the disc, positioned so its closed side will face your body, and clamped tight; check flanges and spindle threads are clean and sound.
Fit the inner flange on its key, seat the disc concentric on the flange pilot, and thread on the outer nut with the correct face against the disc for its thickness and profile.
Press the spindle lock only with the wheel stationary, and tighten the nut firmly with the pin spanner — snug, not maximal force.
Confirm the disc turns freely, does not touch the guard, and sits square with no visible wobble when rotated by hand.
Reconnect power, stand aside out of the disc's plane with the guard opening pointed away from everyone, and run the tool at full speed for thirty seconds to a minute as a test.
If you feel vibration or wobble, stop, re-seat the disc, and discard it if the shake persists; only a smooth-running disc goes to work.

sections.heading: Basic Grinding Technique: Angles, Pressure, and Letting the Disc Work
sections.body:
Good grinding technique reduces to a handful of physical principles, and once you hold them, the tool becomes predictable. The first is the working angle. A depressed-center grinding wheel cuts with the outer band of its face, and it is designed to meet the work at a shallow angle — twenty to thirty degrees is the standard guidance for stock removal. Held near-flat (five to ten degrees), the whole face rubs, the wheel skates and chatters, heat soars, and control drops; held steep (forty-five degrees and up), the wheel's edge digs, gouging crescents into the work and wearing the disc to a mushroomed edge. Flap discs like it shallower — about ten to twenty degrees for blending — and their forgiving construction is why beginners produce better surfaces with them. Wire cup brushes run nearly flat with only the wire tips touching. Whatever the disc, present it so the point of contact throws sparks and debris away from you, downward and forward, with the guard's closed side shadowing your body.

The second principle is that pressure is the enemy of speed. An abrasive wheel removes material in proportion to rim speed and grain sharpness, not to how hard you shove; leaning on the tool slows the motor (dropping the rim speed it cuts with), overheats disc and work, glazes the abrasive, bogs and stalls the machine, and sets up the jams that cause kickback. The correct feel is the weight of the tool plus a controlled lean measured in a couple of pounds — enough to keep a steady spark stream, never enough to change the motor's note by much. If material is coming off too slowly, the answer is a coarser or fresher disc, a more aggressive grain, or a bigger tool — never more muscle. Listen to the motor: a healthy grind hums steadily; a groaning, sinking pitch is your signal to lighten up.

Third, keep the tool moving and the heat managed. A grinder held in one spot excavates a divot and cooks the metal beneath — steel that turns straw, purple, then blue has been locally overheated, which matters greatly on hardened or tempered parts: overheat a mower blade's or chisel's edge past its temper (blue is roughly 300 °C) and it will no longer hold sharpness. Work in smooth overlapping passes along the piece, let the metal cool between passes (a dunk cup for small hardened parts), and take pride in even gray finishes rather than rainbow scorch marks. On welds, grind down to just proud of flush with the hard wheel, then switch to a flap disc to blend flat — chasing flush with a coarse wheel is how good welds get undercut.

Fourth, set up the ergonomics before the trigger. Clamp the work at a height where you can stand balanced, feet apart, elbows comfortably bent, with the grinder's body line such that a kick rotates it past your hip, not into your thigh or face; never grind above your shoulders or overhead if any alternative exists, and never stand teetering to reach. Clear the floor of trip hazards and the cord's path away from the disc. Start the tool off the work, let it reach full speed, then bring it to the metal; lift it off before releasing the switch, and hold it until the disc stops. Sessions tire hands invisibly — vibration numbs grip strength — so break before you are clumsy rather than after.

Last, respect the disc's own rules while you work. Use the face of grinding wheels, the edge of cutting wheels, and never the reverse; do not grind with the disc's unsupported inner region near the flanges; retire wheels worn down near the flange diameter or flap discs worn to the backing plate. A worn-small disc also runs a slower rim speed and cuts poorly — discs are consumables, priced accordingly, and stretching a dying disc is false economy with a failure mode measured in fragments. Fresh disc, shallow angle, light hand, steady motion: that is the whole art, and everything else is practice on scrap.

sections.heading: Cutting Safely: Kickback and How to Avoid It
sections.body:
Cutting is the grinder's most dangerous mode, and kickback is the reason. Kickback is the violent reaction that occurs when the spinning disc is suddenly pinched, snagged, or stalled in the cut: the wheel's momentum and the motor's torque have to go somewhere, and if the disc cannot turn, the tool itself rotates — snapping up and back around the point of contact, toward the operator, in a few hundredths of a second. No human reflex intervenes in that time; whatever grip and body position existed at the moment of the jam is all the protection there is. Severe grinder injuries — deep cuts to thighs, hands, faces, and necks — are overwhelmingly kickback injuries during cutting, often in the last second of a cut, and understanding the mechanics is the best inoculation.

The first defense is managing the cut so the kerf never closes on the blade. Metal and masonry move as they are cut: a bar sagging as it is severed pinches the top of the kerf; a piece supported at both ends closes the cut in the middle; internal stresses in rebar and structural steel grab blades unpredictably. So support the work so the kerf opens as the cut completes — overhang the waste end off the support so its weight pulls the cut open, never bridge the cut between two supports — and clamp the kept piece so nothing shifts. Cut in the orientation that lets gravity help, plan where the freed piece will fall (not on your feet, not pinching the disc as it goes), and on deep sections, make progressive shallow passes rather than burying the disc. A thin cutting disc should slice with its rim only, square to the work: any twisting, prying, or steering in the kerf loads it sideways, and side-loading is both the jam-maker and the disc-snapper. Let the disc reach full speed before entering the cut, feed with light steady pressure, and if the pitch bogs, ease off — a slowing disc grabs.

The second defense is body geometry decided in advance. Hold the tool with both hands, side handle fitted; stand so that neither your body nor your limbs lie in the plane of the disc — off to the side of the cut line, never straight behind it — and position the tool so its kick arc sweeps past you, not through you. Never cut between your legs or braced against your knee; never hold the workpiece in one hand and the grinder in the other; never reach the tool across your body or work above shoulder height. Keep the cut where you can see it without leaning into the disc plane. These habits cost nothing and they decide outcomes: the same jam that bruises a well-positioned operator lacerates a badly positioned one.

The third defense is the equipment configuration this guide has already argued for: a cutting guard that wraps the wheel for cut-off work, a paddle switch that dies when your grip does, an anti-kickback clutch or electronic cutout if your budget allows (they sense the sudden deceleration of a jam and disconnect drive), and a brake that stops the wheel promptly when you release. Thin, fresh, correctly rated discs cut with less force and jam less than worn or wrong ones; a 1 mm to 1.6 mm disc on steel wants almost no pressure at all.

Finally, know the moments kickback loves. The entry, if the disc touches before full speed or skitters across the surface — start against a scored line or a clamped guide. The exit, when the last fibers of metal part and the freed piece shifts — lighten pressure as you feel the cut finishing. The restart in an existing kerf — never re-enter a cut with a spinning disc at an angle; let the disc stop, seat it straight in the kerf, then power on with the tool held firm. And the interrupted cut on embedded material — rebar in concrete, a bolt in a wall — where the disc meets a different material mid-stroke. Treat each of those seconds with full attention, and cutting becomes a controlled, even satisfying operation; treat them casually and the statistics are unforgiving.

sections.heading: Sparks, Dust, and Fire: Managing the Work Area
sections.body:
The grinder's spark stream is beautiful, and it is a running fire hazard measured in meters. Those sparks are white-hot particles of steel and abrasive, leaving the wheel at rim speed; the stream carries ignition-capable material three to five meters, and stray particles bounce and roll further, into corners, cracks, and containers. Fire services in every industrialized country attribute a steady toll of structure fires to hot work — grinding, cutting, welding — and the characteristic feature of those fires is delay: the spark lands in sawdust, cardboard, oily rags, dry grass, or insulation, smolders invisibly for minutes to hours, and flames long after the tool is packed away. That delay is why professional hot-work permit systems require a fire watch during and after the work — commonly thirty to sixty minutes of checking the area once the sparking stops — and it is a discipline worth copying whole into home practice: before you grind, clear or shield everything combustible within five meters; while you grind, know where the stream is going (never into cracks, drains, walls, or piles you cannot inspect); and after you grind, patrol the area, touching and smelling, on a timer, for at least half an hour.

Set the stage before the first spark. Work outdoors or in a cleared area of the shop, on a non-combustible surface — bare concrete, not a wooden bench strewn with shavings; sweep first, because floor litter is the classic first fuel. Move fuel cans, solvent bottles, propane cylinders, aerosols, and the shop vacuum (its dust-laden interior is a fine ignition chamber) well out of the fan of the stream, and never grind near open flammable liquids or their vapors — vapors flash from a single spark. Keep an extinguisher rated for your surroundings within reach (an ABC dry-chemical unit is the versatile choice; water handles smoldering wood and grass), and a bucket of water or a hose adds cheap insurance outdoors. Mind the sparks' effect on things that do not burn, too: the stream embeds hot steel into window glass and etches car paint and pits glazed tile at surprising range — point it away from anything you value, and screen with metal sheet or welding blankets, not plastic tarps, which melt and burn.

Dust is the slower hazard sharing the same air. Metal grinding throws coarse dust that mostly settles, but masonry cutting is another category: dry-cutting concrete, brick, stone, or tile with a diamond blade produces clouds of respirable crystalline silica, invisible at the sizes that matter, which scar lungs permanently (silicosis) and raise lung cancer risk with cumulative exposure. Occupational rules treat it accordingly, and a home project deserves the same controls: cut wet where feasible (a helper with a gentle water stream on the cut, or a tool with water feed — with attention to electrical safety and GFCI protection), or fit a dust shroud connected to a HEPA-filter vacuum, work outdoors upwind, and wear a well-fitted P100/FFP3 respirator regardless, because controls reduce rather than eliminate the cloud. Keep bystanders — especially children — away and downwind-clear; silica does not care whose lungs it enters. Old painted surfaces add lead risk (pre-1978 paint in the US): test before grinding paint, and if lead is present, stop — that job needs containment methods a grinder does not offer.

Finally, manage the human perimeter. A grinder throws debris and, in the worst case, fragments in the disc's plane; bystanders should stand out of that plane and behind the operator's line, ideally behind a screen, and anyone in the area shares the operator's need for eye and ear protection. Cordon the sparks' landing zone from foot traffic, keep pets indoors, and end every session the same way: tool unplugged, disc stopped and cooling somewhere non-combustible (a fresh-cut edge and a used disc are both burn-hot), floor patrolled, and the half-hour fire watch honored. The grinder's acute dangers get the attention, but the fire it leaves behind and the dust it leaves within are the hazards with the longest reach.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and How Discs Fail
sections.body:
Most grinder incidents are not freak events; they are a short list of known mistakes, each with a known failure mode, and walking the list is the fastest safety course available. The first and worst: side-loading a cutting disc. Thin cut-off wheels have enormous strength in their plane and almost none across it — grinding on their flat face, twisting them in a kerf, or prying with them cracks the resin bond, and the crack completes at rim speed, turning the disc into two or three fragments departing at up to 80 meters per second. Every disc maker prints the prohibition; every abrasive-safety body repeats it; and emergency departments keep seeing it. Cut with cutting discs, grind with grinding discs, and if one tool must do both jobs, change the disc — it takes ninety seconds.

Second: over-speeding. Mounting a disc rated below the tool's rpm — classically a big 230 mm wheel on a fast small grinder, guard removed to clear it — loads the wheel past its burst margin, since centrifugal stress grows with the square of rim speed. Bursts from over-speeding are the catastrophic end of the failure spectrum and the reason the speed marking is the first thing you read on any disc. Related: running damaged or expired wheels. A dropped disc, a wheel stored damp for years, a rim chipped against a vise — each carries a hidden crack or a weakened bond, and the ring test, visual inspection, expiry date, and a ruthless discard habit are the whole defense. Discs cost little; treat any doubt as disposal.

Third: guard and handle removal, covered earlier but restated here because it compounds every other failure — the guard is what turns a burst from a tragedy into a scare, and the side handle is what turns a kickback from a laceration into a lurch. Fourth: wrong disc for the material — metal wheels glazing on stone, masonry wheels loading with aluminum until they run unbalanced and hot, ordinary wheels contaminating stainless, wood attacked with toothed carving wheels by unpracticed hands. Fifth: the unclamped workpiece, held in a hand or a knee, which either escapes as a projectile or draws the wheel across the flesh holding it. Sixth: the loaded, glazed, or mushroomed disc pushed harder instead of replaced — pressure is how glazing becomes stalling and stalling becomes kickback. Seventh: setting the tool down while the disc freewheels, letting it walk off the bench or across a thigh; and its cousin, carrying a running grinder. Eighth: disc changes with the battery still in — a bumped paddle switch with fingers at the spindle. Ninth: cutting toward yourself, in line with the disc plane, or above shoulder height, which puts the kickback arc through your face. Tenth: no eye protection for just one cut — the single most cited factor in grinder eye injuries.

It is worth knowing how a disc telegraphs distress, because failures often warn. New vibration or chatter means imbalance — stop, inspect, re-seat, or discard. A changed sound, a wobble visible at speed, a disc that has worn lopsided or small, flap discs showing backing plate, wire wheels shedding heavily, a burnt-resin smell, or a rim that has heat-discolored: each is a disc telling you its bond or balance is going. The response is always the same and always cheap: stop, remove power, and replace it. Add the honest human factors — fatigue, hurry, awkward positions, one more cut at the end of a long day — and you have the actual accident recipe as insurers and safety agencies record it. The grinder rewards a small set of unconditional habits precisely because its failures are fast: rated fresh discs, right disc for the job, guard on, two hands, clamped work, glasses and shield, battery out for changes. None of the ten mistakes above survives contact with that list.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance of the Tool
sections.body:
An angle grinder is a simple, hard-living machine — a universal motor, a gearbox, a spindle, and switchgear, all marinating in the abrasive dust the tool itself creates — and a little deliberate care roughly doubles its life while keeping its safety systems honest. The central enemy is that dust. Grinding swarf is conductive metal grit and abrasive powder, and the motor's cooling fan pulls it straight through the windings; enough of it abrades insulation, packs the air vents, and wears the commutator and brushes. The single most valuable habit is therefore ventilation hygiene: after dusty sessions, with the tool unplugged, blow out the vents and motor housing with dry compressed air (outdoors, wearing your eye and lung protection — you are re-aerosolizing everything the tool ate), brushing stubborn packing loose with a dry paintbrush. Never block vents in use with a wrapped hand or a rag, and avoid grinding directly above the tool's own intake path.

Brushed motors — still the majority of corded grinders — carry a pair of carbon brushes that wear as consumables. Symptoms of tired brushes are weakening power, excessive sparking visible through the vents, a crackling arc smell, and intermittent cutting out; many grinders have external brush caps that make replacement a five-minute screwdriver job with an inexpensive manufacturer-spec pair, and some models feature auto-stop brushes that kill the motor before a worn brush can score the commutator. Brushless cordless models eliminate the wear item entirely, at the price of electronics that dislike deep dust baths just as much. The gearbox — the right-angle bevel gears in the head — runs in grease for the life of the tool in home use; if a high-mileage grinder grows loud, whiny, or hot at the head, a service shop can repack it with the specified grease, and that noise check belongs in your habits, because a howling gearbox and a growing wobble at the spindle are how heads announce bearing wear. Any perceptible play in the spindle — grab the (unpowered) disc and rock it — is a stop-using-and-service condition, since spindle wobble both ruins work and stresses discs toward failure.

Inspect the parts that keep you safe with the same regularity you would give a ladder. The cord and plug: nicks, abrasion (grinders chew their own cords when users let the cable drift near the disc), loose strain relief — a damaged cord is a replace-now item, not a tape job, and cordless users should check battery contacts and pack condition instead. The switch: a paddle that sticks, a lock that engages unexpectedly, restart protection that no longer protects — switchgear faults on a grinder are disqualifying until repaired. The guard: present, undented, clamping firmly, not rattling loose. Flanges and the pin spanner: flat, clean, threads good; a mangled outer nut gets replaced, not persuaded. Side handle threads: intact, handle tight. Any drop of the tool onto concrete earns a full inspection, exactly like a dropped disc.

Storage and records close the loop. Store the grinder dry, ideally in its case, with the disc removed or at least the tool resting so the disc bears no load; store discs flat, dry, indoors, sorted by type, with their labels legible and resin wheels within date — a shoebox lid marked with purchase dates costs nothing. Wipe the tool down after wet-cutting adventures immediately, because grinding dust plus moisture is a rust paste. Before each session, run the thirty-second pre-flight this whole guide implies: cord or battery good, vents clear, guard set, handle tight, correct fresh disc rated and mounted, spanner accounted for (not left threaded on the spindle — a classic), PPE on, work clamped, area cleared. It reads long and takes half a minute, and it is exactly the difference between owners whose grinders die young and hurt people and owners whose grinders bore their grandchildren.

sections.heading: Home Projects Where the Angle Grinder Earns Its Keep
sections.body:
The best way to consolidate everything above is to see the grinder applied to the jobs a homeowner actually meets, because each project exercises a specific disc, technique, and safety discipline. The classic first job is the seized bolt or rusted fastener: a gate hinge bolt rounded beyond any wrench, a rusted exhaust clamp, a padlock with a lost key. A 1 mm cutting disc slices a bolt shank or nut flank in seconds where penetrating oil and drama failed for an hour. The disciplines here are clamping (never hold the assembly), planning the cut so the freed parts fall clear, protecting the surrounding surface with steel shim or sheet, and remembering the fresh-cut edge is burn-hot and razor-sharp — deburr it with a quick pass of a grinding or flap disc, a courtesy your future self will notice.

Metal repair and fabrication is the grinder's home ground. Cutting angle iron, flat bar, rebar, and pipe to length with a cutting disc and a scored line; beveling edges before welding and dressing the weld after — hard wheel to knock the bead down, flap disc to blend it flush; stripping rust and mill scale with a wire cup or stripping disc before paint. A fence panel repair, a trailer patch, a custom bracket: one tool covers the whole metal side of the job. The disciplines are the cutting-versus-grinding disc separation, the shallow-angle light-pressure grind, heat management so thin sheet does not warp and hardened parts do not lose temper, and the INOX rule if stainless is involved. Sharpening rides along here: mower blades, axes, mattocks, and shovel edges all restore quickly under a flap disc or careful grinding wheel — clamp the blade, follow the existing bevel angle, take light passes alternating sides, keep the edge cool enough to touch (dunk often), and never sharpen anything held in your hand.

Masonry work brings the diamond blade out. Cutting pavers and bricks to fit a path edge (score all round, then deepen, or cut halfway and snap with a bolster for thick units); chasing a groove in a wall for conduit; trimming a ceramic or porcelain tile around a pipe with a continuous-rim blade where the tile saw cannot reach; cleaning old mortar off reclaimed brick, and — the repointing job — raking failed mortar joints from a wall with a thin diamond blade or dedicated mortar-raking disc, working to a set depth, ready for fresh pointing. Every one of these is a silica job: outdoors, wet method or shroud-and-HEPA-vacuum, P100/FFP3 respirator fitted properly, bystanders clear. The cut quality disciplines are a marked line, a scored first pass, letting the blade's weight feed, and never twisting the blade in the kerf to steer.

A few jobs deserve a deliberate no, and knowing them is part of owning the tool. Do not use the grinder as a saw for dimensional lumber — a circular saw, jigsaw, or handsaw is faster and safer, and toothed grinder discs are the injury-statistics champion of the accessory world. Do not grind lead paint, do not cut into walls blind (pipes and cables live there — trace first), do not cut galvanized or coated metals in unventilated spaces without a respirator (metal-fume risks are real), and do not freehand-cut anything you cannot clamp. Do not reach for the grinder for jobs a file, a nut-splitter, or an oscillating multi-tool does with a tenth of the energy in play — matching the tool's violence to the job's need is the mature skill. Master the honest jobs on the list above, with the discs, angles, and protections this guide has laid out, and the angle grinder stops being the shop's most feared tool and becomes what professionals know it as: the cheapest, fastest problem-solver on the shelf, dangerous only to people who decline to learn it.
